1. Background

The Republic of the Marshall Islands (RMI) is one of the world's smallest and most isolated nations. The country consists of 29 atolls and 5 low coral islands situated on about 181 square kilometers (km2) of land mass in the Pacific Ocean. Majuro (the nation's capital) and Ebeye, the country's two largest urban centers, account for about 96 percent of the total population, while the remaining inhabitants live on the outer atolls. The Government of the Republic of the Marshall Islands (GRMI) depends mostly on diesel generation to meet the country's growing electricity needs. The country aims to enhance its energy security through renewable energy generation, improve the reliability of electricity supply, enhance energy efficiency, expand e-mobility, and improve access to electricity. Increased energy resilience will reduce dependence on hydrocarbon fuels, insulate the country from the risks of price rises and supply uncertainties, and equip it with natural disaster-resilient electricity infrastructure.

 

MEC, the state-owned energy utility, generates and provides electricity to Majuro Atoll, serving 55 percent of RMI's population. MEC also manages three mini-grids in Jaluit, Wotje, Rongrong (Majuro Atoll), and Kili Island, the latter having been recently transferred to MEC from the Kili Bikini Ejit (KBE) Local Government. Following the integration of the Kwajalein Atoll Joint Utilities Resources (KAJUR) into MEC, MEC is also responsible for power generation and distribution in Ebeye, together with the water and sewerage services previously provided by KAJUR. MEC is responsible for executing plans to enhance energy security but lacks the capability to conceive and implement them. It lacks the funds required to implement these plans. The Government of the Republic of the Marshall Islands (GRMI) has partnered with the World Bank through the Renewable Energy Generation and Access Increase Project (REGAIN) – an IDA grant of US$60 million approved and effective as of December 13, 2024, with a closing date of September 30, 2030. The REGAIN project aims to increase renewable energy generation and improve access to electricity while reducing reliance on diesel-based generation through funding and technical support.

 

RMI’s Electricity Roadmap targets net-zero greenhouse gas emissions and 100% renewable electricity by 2050. As a small and geographically dispersed island nation, RMI remains highly dependent on imported diesel for electricity generation, exposing the country to high energy costs and vulnerability to global fuel price shocks and supply disruptions. To manage this risk, RMI needs to diversify its electricity supply portfolio by integrating more RE, manage demand growth by promoting efficient electricity use, pursue new business opportunities such as EVs, and monitor and report implementation status to the GRMI for appropriate course correction. Ensuring a reliable, clean, and cost-effective electricity supply is therefore critical to achieving national climate commitments, strengthening energy security, and supporting sustainable socio-economic development. The country lacks the legal, policy, and regulatory framework, institutional capability, and the trained manpower required to achieve these objectives. The GRMI has taken some steps in this direction, such as the notification of the Energy Act 2025, which provides a legal, policy, regulatory, and organizational framework to promote security, safety, reliability, and sustainability of energy supply for the benefit of RMI’s economy and citizens and to promote the efficient use of energy and of energy from indigenous sources.

 

Under Sub-Component 3.1 of the REGAIN project (Sector Development Assistance), MEC plans to seek consultancy support from a firm to propose a roadmap and undertake proposed activities for the Implementation of the Energy Act (IEA) 2025.  In the roadmap, IEA shall propose activities to be undertaken in the short, medium, and long term and undertake them to strengthen the capacity of key energy sector stakeholders by focusing on regulation, target setting, monitoring tools, dissemination of progress, feedback, and course correction to promote security, safety, reliability, and sustainability of energy supply in RMI.

 

IEA shall be prepared in close coordination with the newly established National Energy Authority (NEA) and MEC.

 

IEA shall take into account all Acts, policies, regulations, studies and current practices relevant to electricity (all RE included), Energy Efficiency, E-mobility and their funding, including but not limited to:

 

  • Energy Act 2025
  • National Energy Authority Act, 2025
  • Recommendations contained in Integrated Resource and Resilience Plan 2024-2034
  • Electricity Roadmap of 2018, which provides a relevant and guiding framework for the sector’s development
  • MEC’s current tariff methodology and tariff model, prepared by MEC’s Supplemental Management and Operations (SMO) consultant under ADB-funded technical assistance, which covers MEC’s operations prior to the integration of KAJUR and on which the tariff review under Task 6 shall build
  • National Targets and the progress achieved against them to date
  • Relevant energy sector programs and studies of other development partners active in the RMI, in particular the Asian Development Bank (ADB), such as the Energy Transition Project, should be taken into account to ensure coordination and avoid duplication.

 

The assignment will support GRMI, MEC, and NEA in translating the Energy Act, 2025, and the National Energy Authority Act, 2025, into an actionable implementation plan for renewable energy, energy efficiency, and e-mobility. The assignment will identify required policy, regulatory, institutional, monitoring, and capacity-building actions, while excluding provisions related to the petroleum sector. This support aligns with REGAIN’s institutional strengthening objectives and RMI’s need to reduce reliance on diesel, improve energy security, and support the integration of renewable energy.

2. Objectives

The objective of the assignment is to prepare a practical, time-bound implementation plan for renewable energy, energy efficiency, and e-mobility under the Energy Act, 2025, and the National Energy Authority Act, 2025, excluding petroleum-sector provisions, and to support the preparation of priority policy, regulatory, institutional, monitoring, and capacity-building instruments required for implementation.

 

  • Institutional strengthening for the implementation of RE, EE, and e-mobility provisions.
  • Policy and regulatory framework, guidelines for the development of higher RE integration, EE promotion, and e-mobility uptake.
  • Monitoring and reporting framework for RE, EE, and e-mobility targets, progress, and implementation gaps.
  • Database/reporting arrangements for RE, EE, and e-mobility information.
  • Capacity development strategy for institutions, utilities, and local manpower.

3. Project Description

This assignment is financed by the World Bank under the institutional strengthening and implementation support activities of REGAIN. It will support the policy, regulatory, institutional, monitoring, and capacity-building measures required to implement the RE, EE, and E-mobility provisions of the Energy Act, 2025, and the National Energy Authority Act, 2025.

4. Implementation Arrangements

 MEC will be the Employer and the contracting authority for this assignment, responsible for approving deliverables and payments. The Consultant may proceed to the next deliverable under MEC's general guidance. NEA, as the statutory authority responsible for regulating the energy sector, shall be responsible for the technical and regulatory approval of policy- and regulation-driven deliverables. MEC, as Employer, retains ultimate authority for administrative and financial approval and for the release of REGAIN project funds, which shall follow NEA's technical sign-off on the relevant deliverable. The responsible ministry and Cabinet shall be consulted where recommendations require policy approval, regulatory adoption, statutory action, budget allocation, or cross-government implementation. MEC shall be responsible for formal approval of all deliverables and payments. The Consultant shall work under the direction of MEC and coordinate closely with:

 

  • MEC management and technical staff
  • REGAIN Project Management Services Consultant, as applicable
  • Project Implementation Unit (PMU) within MEC
  • NEA, the national regulatory body, serving as the regulatory interface between MEC and the Consultant
  • Responsible Ministry and Cabinet on policy formulation
  • World Bank on matters requiring no-objection, reporting, or implementation support
  • ADB and other development partners active in RMI's energy sector, as relevant

Petroleum-sector implementation matters are excluded from this assignment.

5. Scope of Services

The scope of services is limited to the electricity sector, in particular renewable energy, energy efficiency, and e-mobility, including relevant non-petroleum legal, policy, regulatory, institutional, monitoring, enforcement, data, and capacity-building provisions necessary for their implementation. Petroleum sector related provisions of the Energy Act, 2025, are excluded from the assignment. While MEC is the Contracting Employer for the entire assignment, NEA serves as the primary technical Client for Tasks 1, 2, 3, and 7, given their statutory and regulatory content. MEC's approval of these deliverables is administrative and financial and follows NEA's technical acceptance.

 

  • Task 1: Diagnostic review of the Electricity Sector (in particular RE, EE and E-Mobility) of the Marshall Islands

The Consultant shall review and map the existing institutional arrangement, policy, and regulatory framework against the provisions and the directions contained in the Energy Act (EA) 2025 and the National Energy Authority (NEA) Act 2025 (harmonious reading) for the development of Renewable Energy (RE), Energy Efficiency (EE), and E-Mobility (E-MB). The Consultant will propose a strategy to address misaligned or missing institutional arrangements, policies, and regulatory framework.

  1. Review of existing applicable  policies, strategies, plans, and studies in the context of the requirements of EA 2025 and NEA Act 2025,
  2. Identify whether the gap is institutional, policy, or regulatory, whether it will be addressed within the existing framework (alignment/modification), or whether a new framework is to be created, and
  3. Recommend a broad policy, regulatory, and Institutional framework to address these gaps.

 

  • Task 2: Strategic review of the applicable RMI’s electricity sector related international and national commitments and targets

The Consultant will undertake a focused review of the GRMI's international commitments, national targets, initiatives for the development of RE, EE, and E-MB, and the progress achieved. The diagnostic and strategic review will include the following:

  1. Discussion with the stakeholders and ascertaining reasons for the shortfall in the envisaged progress,
  2. The Consultant shall review relevant national targets, international commitments, ongoing initiatives, and selected comparable Pacific/SIDS practices for RE, EE, and e-mobility implementation. The purpose of the review shall be to identify practical options for policy, regulatory, institutional, monitoring, and capacity-building measures suitable for RMI,
  3. Identification of implementation gaps, in particular critical legal, policy, regulatory, and institutional gaps, which impacted the achievements of these initiatives and targets,
  4. Assess whether these legal, policy, and regulatory gaps stem from implementation shortfall or a missing framework, and
  5. Recommend a broad policy, regulatory, and institutional framework to address these gaps.

 

  • Task 3: Propose a strategy for addressing the identified gaps 

The Consultant will propose a strategy with a time-bound implementation roadmap for addressing the gaps identified in Tasks 1 and 2. The proposed strategy will include the following:

  1. Identification of Implementation gaps, i.e., the framework/provision exists but has not been implemented, or there is a shortfall in its implementation,
  2. Identification of gaps in the existing framework, i.e., the legal, policy, regulatory, or Institutional framework provides for the enabling provision, but it has not been enacted or notified; indicate whether it is a policy, regulatory, or institutional issue,
  3. Identify misalignment (even a section or provision of it) of the policy, regulatory framework, or the institutional framework with the EA 2025 and NEA 2025,
  4. Identification of gaps that cannot be dealt with by the existing framework,
  5. Recommendation of a strategy to deal with these identified gaps. The proposed strategy will indicate the required interventions (legal, policy, regulatory and institutional), their implementation order, the stakeholders responsible for addressing them and the timelines within which these will be addressed (short term- within 3 months, medium term- within 6 months and long term-within 12 months) duly aligned with the statutory timelines provided in the Acts and related policies,
  6. Indicate how the recommended interventions will address the identified gaps.
  7. Indicate the way forward for the gaps which cannot be addressed under the existing legal framework, and
  8. Develop a comprehensive implementation roadmap considering the recommendations made in Task 2 and in this Task, and compile the recommendations.

 

The roadmap should indicate:

  • Short-term actions,
  • Medium-term actions,
  • Long-term actions,
  • Responsible institution,
  • Required decision or instrument,
  • Dependency,
  • Level of priority, and
  • Whether the consultant will draft the instrument under this assignment.
  • Task 4: Assessing the Institutional structure and the manpower requirements of the sector

The Consultant will examine whether the current institutional structure, including its roles and responsibilities, aligns with those prescribed in the Energy Act and is conducive to the development of RE, EE, and E-MB in RMI. The Consultant will examine the following:

  1. Clarity in their role and responsibilities (without any overlap) for the development of RE, EE, and E-MB,
  2. The institutional capacity to lead the development of RE, EE, and E-MB in RMI, such as project planning, design, implementation, operation, and maintenance, and
  3. Recommendations for addressing institutional alignment of roles and responsibilities, capacity gaps, and the coordination mechanism between them for the development of RE, EE, and E-MB, taking into account the integration of KAJUR’s operations into MEC.

 

The Consultant will also assess the skills and the manpower required for the development of RE, EE, and E-MB in RMI. The Consultant shall assess:

  1. Manpower and the skills available with all important stakeholders,
  2. Assess the manpower and the skill requirements considering the national targets and the evolving (proposed Roadmap) legal, policy, regulatory and institutional framework for the development of RE, EE and E-MB for the next 5 years,
  3. Indicate the gaps between availability and requirements, and
  4. Prepare a strategy to meet this gap, indicating the number, the skill requirements, and how the required skills will be met (contents of the training, how and where the training will be provided, suggestions for international collaboration, certification).

 

 

 

  • Task 5: Monitoring, Database and Reporting Framework for RE

The Consultant will assess the status of the RE database to determine its suitability for publishing a report that records, documents, and shares critical information on RE, EE, and E-MB. The Consultant will:

  1. Evaluate the existing database and identify the missing indicators/information gap/data field necessary for various stakeholders to discharge their roles and responsibilities for the development of RE, EE, and E-MB in the country (covering Majuro, Ebeye and the outer island systems),
  2. Recommend formats, information to be gathered, sources of this information, reporting institutions, reporting frequency, and validation process,
  3. Recommend the structure of the report to be published, and
  4. Prepare the first RE encompassing the above recommendations, which NEA can subsequently update and improve upon.

 

  • Task 6: Electricity tariff review and recommendations

The tariff review shall build on, and not duplicate, MEC’s current tariff methodology and tariff model prepared by the SMO consultant. It shall focus on how that methodology has performed in practice, on areas it did not examine in depth, and on extending it to all systems now operated by MEC, including Ebeye following the integration of KAJUR’s operations into MEC, which was not covered by the earlier work. The review shall also provide MEC and NEA with a clear, evidence-based rationale and supporting calculations for the recommended tariff options, so that they are well prepared to respond to tariff proposals from policymakers, investors and other stakeholders.

 

The Consultant shall review the existing electricity tariff arrangements and prepare recommendations and an implementation pathway that are consistent with the Energy Act, 2025, and the National Energy Authority Act, 2025. The Consultant shall, in particular:

  1. Assess the adequacy of the current tariff level, structure, adjustment mechanisms, billing arrangements and related subsidy or compensation mechanisms;
  2. Assess the revenue requirement and efficient cost of electricity service, based on verified utility financial, operational and investment data;
  3. Determine the extent to which prevailing tariffs and practices align with the principles contemplated under the relevant sections of the Energy Act;
  4. Assess tariff implications of planned renewable energy, EE, E-mobility, battery storage, network, resilience and access investments;
  5. Recommend refinements to the existing tariff methodology, tariff structure, adjustment mechanism and regulatory review process that NEA can use in tariff determinations;
  6. Review the application of MEC’s current tariff methodology and identify any issues, anomalies or unintended outcomes that have emerged in practice and that may require adjustment;
  7. Extend the revenue-requirement and cost-of-supply analysis to Ebeye following the integration of KAJUR’s operations into MEC, including harmonization of KAJUR’s financial, operational and customer data with MEC’s, clear separation of electricity costs from water and sewerage costs, and options and a transition pathway for bringing Ebeye’s electricity tariff into MEC’s tariff framework;
  8. Assess the merits and implications of the planned introduction of a single tariff for all customer classes;
  9. Assess whether a uniform national tariff should be maintained across all MEC-served systems (Majuro, Ebeye and the outer islands), or whether location-specific tariffs or tariff adjustment factors are warranted, including the resulting cross-subsidies between locations;
  10. Using the known sizes and costs of the hybrid and mini-grid systems to be installed in the outer islands, estimate the indicative cost of supply and potential tariff for each location, and assess the implications of any proposal to reduce tariffs in locations with high renewable energy penetration;
  11. Assess the practicality, timing and customer impact of reducing or removing existing government subsidies, and the alternatives available;
  12. Assess the feasibility of time-of-use tariffs that reflect the different costs of daytime (predominantly solar) and nighttime (predominantly diesel) supply;
  13. Recommend tariffs and charging arrangements for electric vehicle charging;
  14. Assess feed-in tariff, net-metering and power purchase arrangements for privately owned renewable energy systems seeking to export to MEC’s grid, including pricing based on avoided cost, the grid integration, storage and backup costs borne by MEC, and the volume of such generation the grid can accommodate;
  15. Assess the implications of electricity supplied by third parties outside MEC’s networks, such as renewable energy systems at government or private facilities that supply neighboring communities, including the pricing basis and regulatory requirements for such supply, and how differences between their prices and cost-reflective MEC tariffs can be explained and managed;
  16. Assess distributional and affordability implications for customer classes, including vulnerable customers, and identify transparent options for any subsidy or compensation that may be required; and
  17. Provide practical inputs for preparation and future implementation of the National Electricity Tariff and Billing Code.

 

  • Task 7: Addressing the recommendations

Based on the approved recommendations and implementation roadmap under Task 3, and working under the technical supervision of NEA, the Consultant shall identify, prepare, revise or align the policies, regulations, codes, guidelines and other instruments required to give effect to the relevant provisions of the Energy Act, 2025 and the National Energy Authority Act, 2025, excluding petroleum-sector provisions.

The Consultant shall, in particular:

  1. Prepare or align the electricity-sector regulatory instruments identified as necessary under the Acts, including, as applicable, electricity licensing, electricity-sector regulation, Grid Code, service standards, universal service and subsidy-related mechanisms,
  2. Prepare or align the instruments required for renewable energy, including, as applicable, grid integration, renewable IPPs, community renewable-energy projects, rooftop installations and renewable microgrids,
  3. Prepare or align the instruments required for energy efficiency, including applicable standards, labeling requirements, air-conditioning and cooling energy-efficiency requirements, and other EE measures required to implement the applicable provisions of the Acts,
  4. Prepare or align the instruments required for e-mobility, including applicable requirements relating to charging infrastructure, technical standards, charging services, electricity supply and tariff arrangements, and other matters required to implement the applicable provisions of the Acts, and
  5. Propose the institutional framework and clearly define the roles and responsibilities of the relevant institutions for implementation.

 

6. Qualifications, Tasks, and Level of Effort of Specified Key Experts

The Consultant shall propose a team adequate for the assignment. In its proposal, the Consultant shall specify:

  • The name of the proposed expert, where available,

7. Fees and Reimbursable Expenses

As this engagement will be structured as a lump-sum contract, the selected Consultant shall submit a financial proposal (in addition to a technical proposal) that includes:

  • A total lump-sum price for the performance of the services, payable against the deliverables set out in Section VIII, supported by a breakdown of professional fees by each proposed expert and personnel category, indicating the applicable unit rates and estimated level of effort (person-months or person-days), provided for information purposes; and
  • Reimbursable expenses, included within the lump-sum price, covering any anticipated travel, accommodation, per diem, logistics, communications, and other project-related costs necessary for the performance of the services.

The lump-sum price shall be inclusive of all costs necessary for the performance of the services. The Consultant shall clearly state the assumptions underlying the proposed costs and provide sufficient detail to allow MEC to assess the reasonableness of the proposed budget.

8. Deliverables

The project has six (6) main deliverables.

 

The Consultant shall prepare and submit the following deliverables in accordance with the Scope of Services. The Task references identify the principal Tasks contributing to each deliverable and shall not limit the Consultant's obligation to take into account relevant findings and recommendations arising from other Tasks.

  1. Deliverable 1: Inception Report (Linked to: Tasks 1 to 7)

The Consultant shall submit an Inception Report confirming its understanding of the assignment, methodology, work plan, stakeholder engagement arrangements, data and information requirements, and detailed schedule for carrying out the seven Tasks and submitting the required deliverables.

An Inception Workshop shall be conducted with MEC, NEA, and other relevant stakeholders, and agreed outcomes shall be reflected in the final Inception Report.

The Deliverable shall be submitted within two weeks of Notice to Proceed (NTP).

  1. Deliverable 2: Diagnostic Assessment and Implementation Roadmap (Linked to: Tasks 1, 2 and 3)

The Consultant shall prepare a consolidated Diagnostic Assessment and Implementation Roadmap for the relevant provisions of the Energy Act, 2025, and the National Energy Authority Act, 2025, relating to renewable energy, energy efficiency, and e-mobility.

The deliverable shall consolidate the diagnostic and strategic reviews, identify and categorize the principal implementation, policy, regulatory, and institutional gaps and misalignments, and establish a prioritized, time-bound roadmap to address them.

The roadmap shall identify responsible institutions, required actions, sequencing, dependencies, priorities, and the policies, regulations, codes, and guidelines to be prepared or aligned under this assignment.

The Deliverable shall be submitted within ten weeks of the NTP.

  1. Deliverable 3: Institutional and Capacity Development Framework (Linked to: Task 4 and relevant institutional findings from Tasks 1 to 3)

The Consultant shall prepare an Institutional and Capacity Development Framework setting out the recommended institutional arrangements, roles and responsibilities, coordination arrangements, manpower and skills requirements, identified capacity gaps, and capacity-development strategy for RE, EE and e-mobility.

The proposed framework shall be consistent with the findings and priorities established under Deliverable 2

The Deliverable shall be submitted within eighteen weeks of the NTP.

  1. Deliverable 4: Monitoring, Database and Reporting Framework and RE Report (Linked to: Task 5)

The Consultant shall prepare the Monitoring, Database and Reporting Framework for monitoring progress in RE, EE and e-mobility, including the recommended database, data collection, validation and reporting arrangements and institutional responsibilities.

The deliverable shall include the recommended database and reporting arrangements and the first RE Report, prepared in a form suitable for subsequent updating by NEA.

The Deliverable shall be submitted within twenty-four weeks of the NTP.

  1. Deliverable 5: Electricity Tariff Review and Recommendations (Linked to: Task 6)

The Consultant shall prepare a stand-alone Electricity Tariff Review and Recommendations Report, presenting the assessment, findings, and recommended tariff and regulatory pathway in accordance with Task 6.

The deliverable shall provide the analytical and regulatory basis necessary to support tariff-related decisions and the preparation or implementation of the applicable tariff and billing regulatory framework.

The deliverable shall also include the updated tariff model in editable form, covering all MEC-served systems including Ebeye, and concise briefing notes setting out the rationale and supporting calculations for the recommended tariff positions, for use by MEC and NEA in policy and stakeholder discussions.

The Deliverable shall be submitted within twenty-six weeks of the NTP.

  1. Deliverable 6: Policies, Regulations, Codes and Guidelines for Implementation of the Energy Act (Linked to: Task 7, informed by Tasks 1, 2 and 3)

Based on the approved recommendations and implementation roadmap, the Consultant shall prepare and/or align the policies, regulations, codes, and guidelines identified as necessary to implement the relevant provisions of the Energy Act, 2025, and the National Energy Authority Act, 2025, within the scope of the assignment.

The deliverable shall comprise the agreed package of new and/or revised policies, regulations, codes and guidelines covering, as applicable:

  • Electricity-sector regulation;
  • Renewable energy;
  • Energy efficiency, including air-conditioning and cooling; and
  • E-mobility.

The policies, regulations, codes and guidelines shall be consistent with the gaps, priorities and sequencing established through the preceding Tasks and agreed with NEA and MEC.

The Deliverable shall be submitted within thirty-two weeks of the NTP.

 9. Contract Duration

The contract duration is 9 months. The expected start date is January 2027. 

10. Evaluation Criteria

The Consultant will be selected using the Consultant’s Qualifications-Based Selection (CQS) method in accordance with the World Bank Procurement Regulations for IPF Borrowers and the REGAIN Procurement Plan. Interested firms shall submit an Expression of Interest (EOI) demonstrating their qualifications and relevant experience. EOIs will be evaluated against the criteria below. The most qualified and experienced firm will be invited to submit a combined technical and financial proposal and, if responsive, to negotiate a contract.

  • Experience preparing energy-sector legal, policy and regulatory frameworks, or implementation plans for energy legislation, including regulations, codes and licensing (35 points)
  • Experience in electricity tariff, cost-of-service and revenue-requirement studies for small island or multi-system utilities, preferably with high renewable energy penetration (25 points)
  • Experience in the Pacific or other Small Island Developing States (25 points)
  • Technical and managerial capability of the firm, including core business, years in business, organization and availability of relevant expertise (15 points)

Total: 100 points

Key experts will not be evaluated at the EOI stage. The qualifications of the proposed key experts set out in Section 6 will be reviewed when the selected firm submits its technical proposal.

11. Inputs to be provided by MEC and NEA

MEC, as the Employer, and NEA, as the technical and regulatory counterpart, shall provide or facilitate timely access to the information, documents, data, personnel, and stakeholders reasonably required for the performance of the Services, to the extent available.

NEA shall:

  • Provide or facilitate access to applicable policies, regulations, codes, guidelines, regulatory instruments, sector targets, reports, databases and other relevant regulatory information,
  • Provide available information on institutional arrangements, regulatory processes, staffing and capacity relevant to the assignment,
  • Facilitate access to relevant officials and stakeholders for consultations and workshops, and
  • Review and provide timely technical comments and acceptance of deliverables submitted to it for review or acceptance.

MEC shall:

  • Provide or facilitate access to relevant technical, operational, customer, commercial, financial and investment information and data, including information required for the tariff review, covering all MEC-served systems including Ebeye (former KAJUR operations), and MEC’s current tariff methodology and tariff model,
  • Provide available plans, studies, reports, databases and information relating to existing and planned RE, EE, e-mobility, storage, and network,
  • Facilitate access to relevant MEC and PMU personnel and stakeholder consultations, and
  • Undertake the contractual, administrative and financial review and approval of deliverables in accordance with the implementation arrangements.

The Consultant shall, as part of the Inception Report, submit a consolidated data and information request specifying the information required, its proposed source, format and required date. The Consultant shall promptly identify material data gaps and propose appropriate alternative sources, assumptions or methodologies where required.

The provision of information by MEC, NEA or any other stakeholder shall not relieve the Consultant of its responsibility for the verification, analysis, adequacy and quality of the Services and deliverables required under the Contract.

The Republic of Uzbekistan has received financing from the World Bank for the implementation of the “Innovative Social Protection System for Social Inclusion of Vulnerable Groups in Uzbekistan” (INSON) Project and intends to apply part of the proceeds to consulting services.

The consulting services involve expert and methodological support for the development and practical application of a risk-based child protection model, including the early identification and assessment of risks, prevention of child-family separation, family support, case management, child reunification and family-based care arrangements, and reduction of institutional care. The assignment includes the development of methodologies, procedures and practical tools, recommendations on the functional and methodological logic of the digital platform, selective field testing, and recommendations for further development of the child protection system.

Expected deliverables include a diagnostic report, methodological models and tools, recommendations on deinstitutionalisation, a field testing report, a final report, and a roadmap for further improvement and scale-up. The assignment will last 12 months under a Time-Based Contract. Work will be predominantly in person in Uzbekistan, including agreed fieldwork as agreed with the Client.

The National Agency for Social Protection under the President of the Republic of Uzbekistan invites qualified individuals (“Consultants”) to express their interest in providing the Services. Interested Consultants should submit a curriculum vitae (CV) detailing their education, relevant professional experience and assignments undertaken (including periods, clients, nature of work and the candidate’s personal role), language proficiency, and willingness to perform the assignment personally, including in-person work and fieldwork in the Republic of Uzbekistan. Employees of firms may also express interest through their employer; however, only the qualifications and experience of the individual Consultant concerned will be considered in the selection.

•  A Master’s degree in Child Protection, Public Administration, Law, Education, Social Policy, Social Work or another relevant field. A PhD degree will be an advantage.

•  At least 10 years of demonstrated professional experience in one or more of the following areas: social policy and social protection; child protection and family support; public administration in the social sector; or the development, implementation and methodological support of social programmes and projects.

•  At least 5 years of demonstrated professional experience in child protection and family support, gained specifically in one or more of the following areas: prevention of social orphanhood and family separation; family placement and family-based care; child reunification; or deinstitutionalisation. This five-year experience forms part of the ten-year requirement above.

•  Demonstrated experience in developing, implementing and scaling up new models and approaches, including working with regional teams, training professionals and supporting organisational change.

•  Experience working with government authorities, international organisations and development partners, as well as preparing expert recommendations to inform management decision-making.

•  Experience in adapting and scaling up successful practices across different regional or national contexts.

•  Professional experience in Europe and Central Asia, including post-Soviet countries, in social protection, child protection, family support or institutional care reform will be an advantage.

•  Demonstrated experience with risk-based approaches and case management in the social sector. Experience in providing methodological support for the digitalisation of social processes will be an advantage.

Third-Party Monitoring Firm for Baxnaano’s Economic Inclusion Window

Background

The Government of Somalia launched the Baxnaano programme in 2019. Implemented by the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (MoLSA), with support from development partners, the Baxnaano programme aims to reduce chronic poverty, strengthen household resilience to shocks, and establish the foundations of a national social protection system. Through its regular and shock-responsive cash transfer windows, Baxnaano has reached hundreds of thousands of poor and vulnerable households throughout Somalia. The programme has also strengthened key social protection delivery systems, including participant targeting, payment delivery, grievance redress mechanisms, and the unified social registry (USR).

Building on these achievements, Baxnaano is now in a new phase supported by the World Bank-financed Building Opportunities and Outcomes in Social Protection and Youth Employment in Somalia (BOOST-YOU) Project (P507433), which deepens coverage, expands the program to four windows, and accelerates the transition to full government ownership and management. In its current phase, to be implemented between 2026 and 2029, Baxnaano operates through four programmatic windows: the Regular Window, the Shock-Response Window, the Early Response Human Capital Window, and the Economic Inclusion (EI) Window.

The EI Window builds on an initial pilot aimed at improving employment outcomes, income generation, and productive livelihoods among poor and vulnerable youth. It supports participants in increasing their productive capacity, improving income-earning opportunities, and strengthening long-term resilience. Baxnaano’s EI Window applies a structured and sequenced package of support along two economic inclusion tracks: 1. Wage employment and labour market integration; and 2. Self-employment and entrepreneurship. For each track, an overview of the support package is listed in Table 1.

 

Table 1: Core Economic Inclusion Interventions, by track

Track

Core Interventions

1. Wage Employment and Labour Market Integration

  • Integrated Skills and Socio-Emotional Skills Training (ISST/SE)
  • Employability and work-readiness training
  • Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET)
  • Apprenticeships and internships
  • Coaching and mentoring, including career guidance and counselling, and psychosocial support
  • Job matching and placement services
  • Employer engagement and labour market linkages
  • Post-placement coaching and retention support

2. Self-Employment and Entrepreneurship

  • Integrated Skills and Socio-Emotional Skills Training (ISST/SE)
  • Entrepreneurship and business management training, including financial literacy training
  • Business plan development
  • Coaching and mentoring, including psychosocial support, and enterprise growth and follow-up support
  • Linkage to microloans through financial institutions
  • Market linkages and value-chain integration

Along both tracks, the EI Window will implement the Virtual Labour Market (VLM) intervention. This pilot will support 250 youth to access emerging cross-border digital employment opportunities (both wage and self-employment) through targeted digital skills development, remote work readiness training, freelancing and gig-economy orientation, digital entrepreneurship support, and linkages to VLM platforms. The pilot will also provide access to online job platforms, digital workspaces, mentorship, and market linkages to help participants compete for cross-border employment and income-generating opportunities in regional and global VLM markets.

The EI Window’s targets young people aged 18 to 29 from households within the bottom 40 percent of the income distribution who are unemployed, have experienced extended periods of unemployment, or are engaged in vulnerable forms of employment. Targeted participants will have education levels up to Form 4, except for participants of the VLM pilot who may have also completed post-secondary education and will have strong English proficiency. Over the project period, the EI Window is expected to reach 25,000 young people, at least 60 percent women and 5 percent people living with disabilities (PWD). The program will reach the target participants in cohorts across the target cities in Somalia.

To ensure effective implementation, accountability, and achievement of results, the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs (MoLSA) will engage an independent Third-Party Monitoring (TPM) firm to verify, assess, and report on the implementation, quality, and results of the EI Window. The TPM firm will provide independent monitoring and validation of programme activities across the identified cities, covering process and result verification, youth participation, service delivery quality, compliance with programme requirements, and adherence to environmental and social standards. The assignment will also include a process evaluation and tracer study to assess programme fidelity, relevance, and performance. These Terms of Reference (TOR) outline the objectives, scope, methodology, and deliverables for the provision of TPM services under Baxnaano's EI Window.

Objective of the Third-Party Monitoring

The overall objective of this consultancy is to provide MoLSA, the World Bank, and other relevant stakeholders with timely, accurate, and independent assurance on programme implementation, output quality, emerging outcomes, the functioning of program processes and systems, and participant experiences. The TPM function will support improved programme oversight, strengthen accountability, identify implementation challenges and risks, and generate actionable recommendations to enhance the effectiveness, efficiency, and impact of the BOOST-YOU Project.

Scope of Work

The TPM approach will pursue the following activities through a combination of regular and periodic, qualitative and quantitative assessment techniques across the target locations:

  • Operational verification: Independently verify that program activities across both tracks and the VLM Pilot are implemented in accordance with the operations manual, activity plans, and agreed standards, covering the full range of economic inclusion interventions. Also assess the quality in the implementation of program activities and delivery of package of support. This will involve regular monitoring and spot-checking throughout the contract period.
  • Payment verification: Independently verify that eligible program participants receive the payments to which they are entitled, such as trainee stipends and transport reimbursements, in accordance with programme guidelines, contractual arrangements, and approved payment schedules.
  • Perception and satisfaction: Conduct annual participant perception and satisfaction surveys or assessments to gauge participant experiences and satisfaction. Conduct community consultations and dialogue sessions with stakeholders to assess perceptions of the BOOST-YOU Economic Inclusion Programme's transparency, fairness, targeting, relevance, and effectiveness, capturing challenges and recommendations to inform programme improvement.
  • Results verification: Verify the accuracy and completeness of reported outputs and intermediate outcomes through direct observation, participant interviews, employer contacts, and data triangulation against the records from the program’s Social Protection Delivery System (SPDS), the program’s management information system.
  • Process evaluation: Assess how and how well the program's delivery systems, operational processes, and coordination mechanisms are functioning across both tracks and the VLM Pilot; identify bottlenecks and implementation constraints; and generate actionable evidence to inform operational improvements and future program design or scale-up decisions.
  • Tracer study: Track a stratified random sample of program participants longitudinally across all tracks from program exit through to 6 months post-graduation, to generate statistically representative evidence on labour market and enterprise outcomes, the quality and sustainability of those outcomes, and the self-reported contribution of specific program components — providing a richer evidence base than routine verification surveys alone and informing future program design and scale-up.
  • Special investigations: When complaints, TPM findings, allegations of non-compliance, or programme data suggest irregularities, fraud, safeguarding concerns, or significant deviations, MoLSA may commission targeted investigations by the TPM firm — encompassing spot checks, site visits, interviews, document reviews, and participant verification across programme sites — with findings and corrective action recommendations reported separately.
  • Monitoring additional indicators for the AI4Pathways initiative for the adaptation and testing of AI-enabled tools for profiling, pathway selection, skills and opportunity matching, tailored online employment and entrepreneurship support of participants.

Detailed activities

Operational verification

Programme Implementation Compliance and Verification

The TPM firm shall regularly assess the extent to which the BOOST-YOU Economic Inclusion Programme is being implemented in accordance with the approved Programme Operations Manual (POM), USR protocols, Environmental and Social Commitment Plan (ESCP), and other relevant project guidelines and operational procedures. This will span the entire implementation cycle, from targeting and enrolment, through delivery of program support, to monitoring and evaluation activities.

The TPM firm shall:

  • Verify compliance with programme targeting, participant selection, enrolment, and onboarding procedures. This will check whether participant targeting, enrolment, verification, and participation processes are implemented in stipulated in the relevant program documents and processes, including the POM, USR, and other approved programme guidelines.
  • Verify compliance of program implementation and delivery in accordance with the POM and other approved program guidelines. This will include checking that implementing partners deliver the package of support in a timely and transparent manner.
  • Verify compliance by all contracted service providers and implementing partners with project requirements and contractual obligations.
  • Monitor and assess the quality of the programme interventions, including the socio-emotional skills training, employability training, technical skills development, entrepreneurship support, business development services, coaching and mentoring, and apprenticeships.
  • Monitor adherence to environmental and social safeguards, including labour management procedures, occupational health and safety standards, stakeholder engagement requirements, grievance redress mechanisms, gender inclusion, disability inclusion, and prevention of Sexual Exploitation and Abuse/Sexual Harassment (SEA/SH).
  • Assess the effectiveness of programme monitoring systems, participant tracking mechanisms, and data management processes.

Programme implementation compliance and verification will combine continuous process monitoring with spot-check visits across all Economic Inclusion interventions implemented by MoLSA, implementing partners, training providers, employers, Mastercraft persons, financial institutions, and other service providers.

Process monitoring will adopt a mixed-methods approach, using Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) and Key Informant Interviews (KIIs) for qualitative data collection, complemented by targeted quantitative surveys to generate evidence on programme implementation, participant experiences, and service quality. Spot-check visits will be conducted at training centres, workplaces, apprenticeship sites, employer premises, business support facilities, and other project-supported locations to verify compliance with approved operational procedures, service delivery standards, and contractual requirements.

Participant Verification and Participation Monitoring

In addition to monitoring compliance and verification in terms of program implementation, the TPM firm will also monitor and verify participant targeting, enrolment, and engagement in the program.  For this, the TPM firm shall:

  • Verify that participants enrolled in the programme meet the approved eligibility criteria and are receiving the services and support outlined under the Economic Inclusion package.
  • Validate participant enrolment and participation records.
  • Regularly verify attendance and participation in all program interventions, such as training, coaching, mentorship, apprenticeship, and employment support activities.
  • Identify and report any inclusion or exclusion errors, duplication, or irregularities in participant enrolment and engagement.

Payment verification

The Payment Verification exercise will provide MoLSA and the World Bank with independent assurance that trainee stipends and transport reimbursements under the BOOST-YOU Economic Inclusion Programme are reaching intended participants accurately, transparently, and in accordance with approved procedures and payment schedules. Verification will cover target locations to be specified by MoLSA.

Specifically, the firm will verify:

  • Whether the firm has paid trainee stipends to eligible participants in approved programme activities, including socio-emotional skills training, technical skills training, entrepreneurship training, and on-the-job training (OJT).

The TPM firm will conduct independent verification using a combination of participant surveys, phone-based verification, field visits, document reviews, and spot checks, covering participant verification surveys to confirm receipt and accuracy of payments, reconciliation of payment records across all relevant parties to identify discrepancies, and unannounced spot-check visits to verify eligibility, documentation, and compliance with approved payment procedures.

Payment verification shall be conducted using a statistically representative sample of participants across the four target cities, covering both tracks, including female participants, persons with disabilities, and other vulnerable groups. Additional samples may be selected based on payment-related complaints received through the Grievance Redress Mechanism (GRM), monitoring findings, or identified risks.

The TPM firm shall provide periodic payment verification reports, either as stand-alone reports or as part of the quarterly reports. See section 7 for more details on the reporting requirements for payment verification.

Perception and satisfaction

Participant Experience Assessment

The objective of the Participant Experience Assessment is to understand participants’ experiences throughout the programme cycle, including targeting, enrolment, orientation, participation in program activities, and exit processes. This assessment will capture participants’ satisfaction with the program as well as their perception on relevance, implementation quality and impact of the programme. Specifically, the assessment will evaluate:

a. Participant satisfaction

  • Satisfaction with the enrolment and targeting process.
  • Satisfaction with the quality and relevance of all program interventions, such as socio-emotional skills training, employability training, technical and vocational skills development, entrepreneurship support, coaching, mentoring, and employment facilitation.
  • Satisfaction with support provided by training providers, employers, master crafts persons, financial institutions, and implementing partners.
  • Satisfaction with payments, including clarity of payment information and communication, timeliness of payments, accessibility of payment services, conduct of payment service providers, ease of accessing transport reimbursement and stipend payments, and overall satisfaction with the payment process.
  • Challenges faced by participants in accessing or participating in programme activities.
  • Satisfaction and experience with grievance redress and feedback mechanisms.
  • Accessibility and inclusiveness of programme interventions for women, youth, persons with disabilities (PWDs), and other vulnerable groups.
  • Satisfaction with communication, outreach, and participant engagement processes.

b. Perceived Outcomes and Benefits

  • Perceptions regarding improvements in employability, technical skills, business knowledge, confidence, and job readiness.
  • Perceived contribution of the programme to employment, self-employment, income generation, and livelihood improvement.
  • Participant views on the relevance of acquired skills to labour market opportunities and business development needs.

c. Social Risks, Safeguarding, and Inclusion

  • Whether participants experienced or observed discrimination, exclusion, harassment, Gender-Based Violence (GBV), Sexual Exploitation and Abuse/Sexual Harassment (SEA/SH), or other social risks associated with programme participation.
  • Participant awareness of safeguarding measures, referral pathways, and available support services.
  • Perceptions regarding fairness, transparency, and inclusiveness of programme implementation.

d. Awareness of Programme Information and Feedback Mechanisms

  • Participant awareness and understanding of programme objectives, eligibility criteria, entitlements, and available support services.
  • Awareness and utilisation of the Grievance Redress Mechanism (GRM) and other feedback channels.
  • Participant confidence in reporting concerns, complaints, and grievances through established mechanisms.

The assessment will be undertaken annually and shall use a quantitative survey, complemented where possible by qualitative tools such as in-depth interviews or FGDs. The survey shall cover a statistically representative sample of participants across the four target cities, disaggregated by gender, age, disability status, intervention pathway, and other categories as agreed with MoLSA. The sampling methodology and sample size shall be subject to MoLSA approval, as part of the inception report.

Survey data collection shall be conducted primarily through face-to-face structured interviews, supplemented by phone interviews where necessary. The survey questionnaire will be developed by MoLSA and may be revised periodically in consultation with the TPM firm to reflect programme priorities and emerging information needs. Process evaluation

The TPM firm shall conduct a process evaluation to investigate how the program is being implemented, why it is working or not working, and what systemic factors are enabling or constraining delivery. Findings shall be synthesized in dedicated process evaluation reports at mid-term and end of assignment. Specifically, the process evaluation will pursue the following objectives:

  • Assess implementation fidelity: the degree to which the program is being delivered as designed, and where and why deviations occur.
  • Identify implementation challenges, operational bottlenecks, system-level constraints in program processes and coordination mechanisms, deviations from programme procedures, or unintended outcomes that may affect programme performance and participant outcomes.
  • Understand participant experience from entry through to outcomes, including the drivers of dropout and barriers to full engagement.
  • Assess the effectiveness of the implementation architecture, including relationships between the PMU, service providers, employer partners, and FSPs.
  • Generate operational learning to inform in-course adjustments and future program design or scale-up.

Annex 1 includes possible questions that may be used to achieve the objectives of the evaluation. To address these, the TPM firm may consider but not be limited to the following methods

  • Key informant interviews (KIIs): Semi-structured interviews with PMU staff, service provider management, trainers, coaches and mentors, employer partners, FSP representatives, and VLM platform liaisons, conducted at least twice per year.
  • FGDs: Separate FGDs with active participants (by track, gender, and city) at program midpoint and completion, and with dropouts where accessible, to understand participant experience and barriers.
  • Dropout analysis: The TPM request from the PMU a dropout register tracking participants who exit before completion, by stage, track, city, and demographic group; conduct interviews with a sample of dropouts to understand causes and document systemic patterns.
  • Participant journey mapping: At inception and mid-term, the TPM shall map the end-to-end participant journey for each track, documenting actual versus intended flows, bottlenecks, and points of friction.
  • Document and data review: Analysis of program progress reports, provider reports, MIS data trends, GRM logs, and coordination meeting minutes to triangulate primary data findings.

The TPM firm shall produce a Mid-Term Process Evaluation Report at the midpoint of the assignment, providing a systematic assessment of all domains, identifying key systemic constraints, and recommending operational adjustments. As part of its end-of-assignment deliverables, the firm shall also produce a Final Process Evaluation Report synthesising all process evaluation evidence, documenting lessons learned by track and component, and providing recommendations for programme continuation, scale-up, or redesign.

Tracer study

The TPM firm shall design and implement a longitudinal tracer study to generate statistically representative evidence on participant outcomes, their quality and sustainability over time, and the factors — including program components — that shape them. This study will track a stratified random sample of program participants from all tracks from the point of program exit through to 6 months post-exit. In this sense, the tracer study is analytically distinct from the result verification exercise described in section 4.4, which is intended to confirm the accuracy of specific reported results for provider performance management purposes.

The objectives of the Tracer Study are to:

  • Measure labour market and enterprise outcomes for program participants at 3 and 6 months post-program exit, at a level of statistical precision sufficient to support program performance reporting and design decisions.
  • Assess the quality and sustainability of outcomes: this includes whether participants are employed or operating a business, and on what terms, at what earnings level, with what trajectory, and with what degree of job or enterprise security.
  • Understand the labour market pathways taken by participants after program exit, including those who changed tracks, moved between wage and self-employment, or left the labour market entirely.
  • Capture the self-reported contribution of specific program components (ISST/SE, TVET, coaching, placement services, FSP linkage, VLM platform access) to outcomes, to identify which elements participants found most valuable and which need strengthening.
  • Document barriers and enablers of sustainable outcomes by gender, disability status, track, city, and VLM vs. non-VLM participation.
  • Generate operational and design learning to inform program continuation, scale-up, and future economic inclusion programming.

Cohort Definition and Sampling Design

The tracer study shall track a stratified random sample of participants drawn from each program cohort as they exit the program. The sample shall be stratified by:

  • Track (Track 1: Wage Employment; Track 2: Self-Employment; VLM Pilot)
  • City ( target cities)
  • Gender (women and men)
  • Disability status (PWD and non-PWD), with deliberate oversampling of PWD given their smaller share of the overall population

The TPM firm shall specify the sample size for each stratum in the inception report.[1] The sample shall be selected at program exit (the baseline contact point for the tracer) from the full participant list for each cohort, using a random selection procedure documented in the inception report. The same individuals shall be tracked across all subsequent rounds; the TPM firm shall implement a systematic attrition management protocol (described below) to maintain adequate response rates.

Data Collection Rounds and Instruments

The tracer study shall comprise three data collection rounds per cohort:

  • Round 0 — Exit survey (baseline): Administered at or immediately after program exit (within two weeks of exit). Captures: track completed, components received, competencies acquired, employment or business status at exit, aspirations and immediate post-program plans, and baseline contact information for follow-up.
  • Round 1 — Three-month follow-up: The primary outcome measurement round. Captures the indicators, including employment status, earnings, job quality, enterprise status and revenue, FSP loan status, VLM platform engagement and earnings, barriers encountered, and self-reported contribution of program components. A more comprehensive list of indicators is included in Annex 2. The TPM firm will need to ensure that the study captures indicators included in the program results framework.
  • Round 2 — Six-month follow-up: Captures the same core outcome indicators as Round 1 to assess trajectory and sustainability over time, with additional questions on skills utilization, career or enterprise development since Round 1, and longer-term outlook. This should be in line with the monitoring, evaluation, and learning framework developed for Baxnaano, under BOOST-You.

The tracer study instrument shall be a structured survey developed by the TPM firm, with separate modules for Track 1, Track 2, and VLM participants. It shall include a mix of closed and open-ended questions, and shall be available for administration by phone, in-person interview, or (for VLM participants with reliable connectivity) online self-completion. The instrument shall be piloted with a small non-sample group of participants before deployment and revised based on pilot findings. The instrument shall be submitted to the PMU team for review and approval before deployment.

Contact Maintenance and Attrition Management

Longitudinal tracking of a young, mobile, urban population requires proactive contact management. The TPM firm shall:

  • Collect a minimum of three contact points per participant at the Round 0 exit survey: the participant's own mobile number, an alternative household contact, and a community-level contact (e.g., a program peer, community leader, or service provider contact).
  • Update contact information at each subsequent round and flag any changes in location or circumstances that could affect future tracking.
  • Coordinate with the program MIS to access updated contact records where available, subject to data protection protocols.
  • Apply a minimum of three contact attempts per participant across different times of day and days of the week before classifying a participant as unreachable at any given round.
  • Maintain an attrition log documenting the reason for non-response at each round (not reachable, refused, relocated, deceased, or unknown), disaggregated by track, city, gender, and disability status.
  • Report attrition rates and any evidence of systematic non-random attrition — which could bias findings — in each tracer study report, and propose remediation measures if attrition exceeds 20 percent in any stratum.

Analysis and Reporting

The TPM firm shall produce four tracer study outputs: a Design Report (submitted with or shortly after the inception report) documenting the sampling protocol, instrument design, attrition management plan, and analysis plan; a Round 1 Report (three-month follow-up) and Round 2 Report (six-month follow-up) for each cohort, both presenting disaggregated statistics, outcome analysis, qualitative synthesis, and comparisons against programme targets, with the Round 2 Report additionally analysing outcome sustainability between six and twelve months; and a Synthesis Report at the end of the assignment pooling data across all cohorts and rounds to present aggregate findings and policy and design recommendations.

All tracer study reports shall include a data quality and attrition section, reporting response rates by stratum and assessing the risk of attrition bias. Findings shall be presented in a format accessible to program management, with an executive summary of no more than four pages, a dashboard of key outcome indicators, and detailed findings with supporting tables in annexes.

Special Investigations

Where complaints, grievances, TPM findings, or programme data indicate potential irregularities, non-compliance, fraud, safeguarding concerns, or significant deviations from expected results, MoLSA may request targeted investigations by the TPM firm. Such investigations may involve additional site visits, stakeholder interviews, document reviews, and participant verification exercises. These investigations may be conducted at any programme location within Mogadishu, Baidoa, Kismayo, or Bosaso and will be reported separately with findings and recommendations for corrective action. For example, where payment-related complaints, anomalies, or suspected irregularities are identified, MoLSA may request that the TPM firm conducts additional verification activities, including participant tracing, record reviews, and field investigations, and provide detailed reports on findings and recommended remedial actions.

Methodology

The firm will propose an appropriate methodology, including the sampling approach and tools to be used, to achieve the expected results within the specified budget. The proposed methodology shall be detailed in the Inception Report. The tools and methods may include a combination of direct observation, participant interviews, key informant interviews, focus group discussions, record reviews, surveys, and other appropriate approaches. For example, these may be used as follows:

  • Spot-check visits. Spot-checks may be conducted across all Economic Inclusion interventions — including participant mobilisation and enrolment, training centres, on-the-job training and apprenticeship sites, employer and master craftsperson placements, entrepreneurship support activities, and delivery of stipends, grants, and toolkits — to verify compliance with programme procedures, service standards, contractual obligations, and safeguards requirements. Each visit could combine direct observation using structured checklists, short interviews with participants, trainees, apprentices, and employers, review of attendance, payment, and business support records, and documentation of any irregularities, non-compliance issues, safeguarding concerns, or deviations from programme procedures.
  • Focus Group Discussions (FGDs). FGDs may be conducted with programme participants and, where relevant, non-participants, disaggregated by gender, disability status, and intervention pathway — including female and male participants, persons with disabilities, and youth in wage employment and self-employment pathways. Each FGD could consist of between 5 and 12 participants. Discussion guides may cover key implementation and participant experience issues while allowing flexibility to explore emerging concerns.
  • Key Informant Interviews (KIIs). KIIs may be conducted with a diverse range of stakeholders, including MoLSA officials, local government representatives, community leaders, implementing partners, training providers, employers and master craftspersons, financial institutions, business development service providers, and GRM personnel. Respondent selection could ensure representation across social, economic, geographic, and institutional perspectives.
  • Review of programme records. The TPM firm may review programme documentation maintained by MoLSA, implementing partners, training providers, employers, and service providers. This could include participant files, attendance records, payment documentation, training materials, grievance logs, and other relevant programme records, with the aim of verifying compliance, identifying discrepancies, and corroborating findings from field-based data collection.
  • Surveys. Quantitative surveys may be administered to a representative sample of programme participants across the four target cities to generate systematic evidence on implementation progress, service quality, and participant experiences. Surveys could be conducted through face-to-face structured interviews, complemented by phone-based methods where necessary, and disaggregated by gender, age, disability status, and intervention pathway.

As part of the proposed methodology, the TPM firm will summarize how it plans to use the different tools across the range of TPM activities, using the template table included in Annex 3.

The TPM firm will develop a sampling framework for the TPM activities across the four target cities. The sampling approach shall include random and risk-based selection of participants, training centres, employers, apprenticeship sites, business support activities, and other programme intervention locations, taking into consideration information received through the Grievance Redress Mechanism (GRM) and programme monitoring systems. The sampling framework will ensure adequate representation of all intervention pathways, target groups, and geographic locations.

Key process evaluation questions, by domain:

Targeting and outreach:

  • Are outreach and recruitment strategies reaching the intended populations, including the most vulnerable youth, young women, and PWD? What barriers prevent uptake among eligible youth who do not enrol?
  • Is the targeting process perceived as fair and transparent by community members and non-participants? Are there tensions or complaints related to selection?
  • Are eligibility criteria fit for purpose, or are they creating unintended exclusion of genuinely eligible youth?

Track design and sequencing:

  • Is the sequencing of interventions (ISST/SE → vocational or entrepreneurship training → placement or enterprise support) logical and manageable for participants? Are transitions between stages well-supported?
  • Are participants appropriately matched to tracks based on their profiles, aspirations, and capacities? Are matching criteria and processes working as intended?
  • Are the duration and intensity of training appropriate for the target population, including those with lower prior education or additional vulnerabilities?

Service provider performance and capacity:

  • Are service providers (training institutions, TVET providers, coaches, mentors) adequately capacitated to deliver as designed? Where are capability gaps most acute?
  • Are coordination mechanisms between the PMU and service providers functioning effectively? Are reporting requirements manageable and data flows timely?
  • What is the quality of coaching and mentoring relationships? Are participants accessing coaches consistently and finding the support useful?
  • Are psychosocial support components well-integrated into the broader package, or are they siloed and underutilized?

Employer engagement and labour market linkages (Track 1):

  • Are employer engagement strategies generating sufficient and appropriate placement opportunities? What are the main barriers to employer participation?
  • Is the quality of apprenticeship and internship placements adequate in terms of supervision, relevance, and skills development? Are employers honouring their commitments?
  • Is post-placement retention support reaching youth effectively? What are the most common causes of early exit from employment?

FSP linkage and financial access (Track 2):

  • Is the FSP linkage model functioning as intended? What is the soft loan uptake rate among eligible participants, and what factors explain non-uptake?
  • Are FSP loan products (terms, amounts, repayment periods) appropriate for early-stage youth entrepreneurs? Are there structural mismatches between product design and participant needs?
  • Do participants have adequate financial capability from the financial literacy training to manage loan obligations responsibly?
  • Are FSPs adequately incentivized and operationally prepared to serve this client segment?

VLM Pilot systems and readiness:

  • Are digital infrastructure and connectivity conditions in the four cities adequate for VLM participation? What are the main technical barriers?
  • Are VLM platform linkages functioning effectively? Are participants able to compete for and secure contracts on linked platforms?
  • What are the main barriers to cross-border earnings (payment infrastructure, language, discrimination, platform access)? How are these being addressed?
  • Is the pilot generating sufficient operational learning for scale-up decisions?

GRM and participant voice:

  • Is the GRM accessible, visible, and trusted by participants? Are participants aware of how to raise complaints and confident that doing so will not affect their program participation?
  • Are GRM cases being resolved in a timely and satisfactory manner? Are systemic issues being fed back into program management?

Gender and inclusion systems:

  • Are gender-differentiated support measures (childcare, transport, flexible scheduling) operationally functional and consistently applied?
  • Are program processes creating or reinforcing barriers for women or PWD at any stage? Where are dropout rates highest by demographic group, and why?
  • Are SEA/SH prevention measures embedded in provider management and workplace engagement, or are they treated as compliance checkboxes?

Key Tracer Study indicators

Track 1 — Wage Employment:

  • Employment status at 3 and 6 months (employed, self-employed, unemployed, inactive), disaggregated by gender, disability status, and city
  • Type of employment (formal wage, informal wage, apprenticeship/internship, casual/daily labour)
  • Monthly earnings at 3 and 6 months, disaggregated by gender
  • Duration of current or most recent employment spell
  • Skills match: extent to which current job uses skills acquired through the program (self-assessed)
  • Job satisfaction and reported working conditions (including harassment or exploitation)
  • Number of job changes since program exit and reasons for change or exit
  • Self-reported contribution of ISST/SE, TVET, coaching, and job placement services to employment outcomes

Track 2 — Self-Employment and Entrepreneurship:

  • Enterprise operational status at 6 and 12 months
  • Monthly revenue and profit trends since exit
  • Number of employees or regular workers (if any)
  • Formalization status (business registration) at 12 months
  • FSP loan uptake: whether a soft loan was taken, amount, repayment status, and perceived adequacy
  • Market linkage status: active buyer or value-chain relationships at 6 and 12 months
  • Self-reported contribution of entrepreneurship training, business plan support, coaching, FSP linkage, and market linkage services to enterprise outcomes

VLM Pilot:

  • Active VLM platform engagement at 6 and 12 months (number of platforms, activity level)
  • Gigs or contracts completed in the 30 days prior to interview
  • Monthly earnings from VLM activities at 6 and 12 months
  • Client diversity (local, regional, global)
  • Barriers to VLM earnings (connectivity, payment infrastructure, language, competition, discrimination)
  • Self-reported contribution of digital skills training, remote work readiness, and platform linkages to VLM outcomes

Cross-cutting (all tracks):

  • Perception of program overall and most valued component
  • Whether the participant would recommend the program to peers
  • Wellbeing indicators (self-reported financial security, confidence, agency)
  • Gender-specific: changes in decision-making power, mobility, and household dynamics since program exit
  • PWD-specific: adequacy of accommodations received and barriers to sustained outcomes
