   . BACKGROUND

Ukraine and the World Bank have signed the agreements for the Program "Lifting Education Access and Resilience in Times of Need in Ukraine Program" (hereinafter referred to as the LEARN). The objectives of the LEARN are: to (i) improve teaching and learning conditions; and (ii) to strengthen the management capacity of the education system.

The total financing for the Operation is US$451 million using a combination of the World Bank's financial instruments: Program-for-Results (PforR) complemented by Investment Project Financing (IPF).

The Program-for-Results (PforR) is funded by a US$235 million credit provided by Bank resources, supported by credit enhancement from the Advancing Needed Credit Enhancement for Ukraine (ADVANCE Ukraine) Trust Fund, which is backed by the Government of Japan. This is formalized under the Financing Agreement between Ukraine and the International Development Association for the Program (CREDIT NUMBER 7626-UA). An additional US$150 million is provided under the Special Program for Ukraine and Moldova Recovery (SPUR) of the International Development Association (IDA) Crisis Facility, as outlined in the Loan Agreement between Ukraine and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development for the Program (LOAN NUMBER 9721-UA). Financing Agreement (Additional Financing: Lifting Education Access and Resilience in Times of Need in Ukraine Program) between Ukraine and the International Development Association (CREDIT NUMBER 7905-UA) was signed in the amount of US$4.9 million.

Furthermore, US$30 million in Investment Project Financing (IPF) is secured under the Grant Agreement between Ukraine and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the International Development Association, acting as the administrator of the Ukraine Relief, Recovery, Reconstruction, and Reform Multi-Donor Trust Fund (URTF GRANT NUMBER TF0C5794).

Furthermore, US$31.1 million in Additional Financing is provided through grant resources, consisting of US$30.0 million from the Ukraine Relief, Recovery, Reconstruction, and Reform Multi-Donor Trust Fund and US$1.1 million from the Global Partnership for Education Fund. This additional financing is formalized under the Grant Agreement between Ukraine and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development and the International Development Association, jointly acting as a Supervising Entity for the Global Partnership for Education Fund and as administrator of the Ukraine Relief, Recovery, Reconstruction, and Reform Multi-Donor Trust Fund (URTF GRANT NUMBER TF0D0612; GPE GRANT NUMBER TF0D0613), and supports activities related to the continued implementation of the Program.

LEARN was developed to address critical challenges and provide essential support to the education sector, aligning with the Ministry of Education and Science's (MoES) Strategic Action Plan.

The Operation will focus on supporting the Strategic Action Plan Priority 2: School education and the New Ukrainian School (NUS). The continuation of the NUS reform is a key priority of the MoES.

The objectives of the Operation are to (i) improve teaching and learning conditions; and (ii) strengthen management capacity of the education system.

For this program, "teaching and learning conditions" refer to three critical factors of education service delivery:

  1. safety, including shelters as a pre-condition for schools to open for in-person learning and free and inclusive school bus transportation for students living further distances from schools;
  2. learning materials, especially updated textbooks and age-appropriate learning materials in line with the NUS model; and
  3. teachers trained on NUS standards, principles, and the use of the updated learning materials.

Meanwhile, "management capacity of the education system" refers to institutional capabilities to plan, allocate, and monitor resources based on robust data at the student and school levels.

The NUS Implementation Office (NIO) was established by the Ministry as an advisory and consultative body. The NIO's primary purpose is to support and implement the New Ukrainian School (NUS) reform by providing expert guidance, strategic oversight, and coordination of reform initiatives across Ukraine.

 

II. OBJECTIVES AND EVALUATION QUESTIONS

Overall objective

 

The overall objective of the assignment is to assess how and under what conditions the inputs and activities of the upper-secondary pilot are delivered and translated into early changes in practice across the 150 pilot lyceums, and to generate evidence for adjustments to the pilot and national scale-up. All eight evaluation thematic areas shall receive descriptive coverage, while in-depth theory-based analysis shall focus on a limited set of priority mechanisms: the money-follows-the-teacher mechanism, school management capacity, management-track professional development, and the materials-approbation feedback loop. The Consultant may propose a justified adjustment to this set at inception, subject to Client approval.

The process evaluation is formative and theory-based. It is not an impact evaluation: learning outcomes are not yet observable at meaningful scale, and the estimation of the effect of the pilot on student outcomes is outside the scope of this assignment. The evaluation shall produce practical findings during the 2026/2027 school year, while adjustments to the pilot and the preparation of the national roll-out are still possible.

Specific objectives

  • SO1. For each evaluation thematic area, establish whether inputs reached the 150 lyceums as intended and were actually usable, distinguishing formal or administrative delivery from verified receipt and use.
  •  
  • SO2. Document implementation variation in early changes in practice across the pilot lyceums and identify plausible drivers associated with implementation practices, management decisions, and structural or contextual conditions.
  • SO3. Examine separately how teacher-level and principal/school leadership-level development are functioning, given that they rely on different inputs, delivery mechanisms (training tracks) and assumptions.
  • SO4. Test the assumptions of the Theory of Change, prioritising those that are currently unverified or contested (in particular the four priority mechanisms defined in the overall objective: the "money follows the teacher" mechanism, school management capacity, management-track professional development and the speed of the materials-approbation feedback loop).
  • SO5. Assess what the implementation-variation findings imply for national scale-up, including which enabling conditions are essential, which constraints can be addressed through additional support or adaptation, and which represent structural limits to the current model.

Key evaluation questions

The evaluation shall answer the following five key evaluation questions. The detailed guiding questions by ToC level and evaluation thematic area, with their links to the specific objectives, their priority level and their primary evidence level, are set out in Annex 2.

  • To what extent have the planned inputs and delivery activities in each evaluation thematic area reached the pilot schools and intended participants on time, and to what extent are they usable and actually used?
  • What early changes in practice can be observed in the pilot schools, how do they vary between schools, and what plausible implementation, management, structural or contextual factors are associated with that variation?
  • How are the teacher-development and the principal/school-leadership development pathways functioning, how do they differ, and how do they interact at school level?
  • Which key assumptions and mechanisms of the Theory of Change hold in practice, in particular the four priority mechanisms ("money follows the teacher", school management capacity, management-track professional development and the materials-approbation feedback loop) and the governance and support cascade,, and which local adaptations preserve or weaken the model?
  • Which enabling conditions are essential, which constraints can be compensated through additional support or adaptation, which represent structural limits to the current model, and what does this imply for the national scale-up?

Upper secondary (profile) education pilot context 

From the 2026/2027 school year, 150 lyceums (hereinafter – pilot schools) selected on a competitive basis are piloting the new model of profile upper secondary education in accordance with the CMU Resolution No. 1058 and the relevant MoES order 1127 from 13.07.2026. Several components of the model are introduced at the same time:

  • legal and regulatory framework, including the requirement to provide profile choice across three clusters within each community;
  • curricula matching the tracks (profiles) selected by the pilot schools;
  • professional development for teachers, including virtual accounts under the "money follows the teacher" mechanism (MoES Order No. 434);
  • a separate management track of professional development for principals and school leadership teams;
  • new programmes and teaching and learning materials piloted together with the UIED;
  • investment in infrastructure, STEM equipment and staffing of the pilot schools;
  • coordination mechanisms run by the NIO, including regular coordination meetings with the pilot schools.

This is the first time the multi-component model is implemented at scale. The earlier pre-pilot in 30 schools was voluntary and not representative. Decisions on the national roll-out of profile education from the 2027/2028 school year require evidence not only on whether the model is delivered, but also on what works, for whom, under which conditions and why.

The MoES already has an administrative and monitoring database on the pilot, including school selection records, institutional identifiers in AIKOM, records of teacher training from the Vector platform, equipment delivery records, and minutes of NIO coordination meetings. The pilot Theory of Change (summarised in Annex 1) defines the expected results chain and key assumptions.

Known limitations

Bidders should assume the following limitations, which the evaluation is expected to address only to the extent specified in these Terms of Reference:

  • Vector records show completion of teacher training but are not linked to the subjects those teachers teach, while the grades they teach and their school affiliations in most cases may be devised, some in a non-trivial way (USREOU-AIKOM identifier mapping);
  • participant-to-school linkage for the management track has not yet been confirmed against the full pilot list;
  • equipment records document delivery, not installation, functionality or actual use;
  • minutes of NIO coordination meetings record requests and decisions but are not independent verification of implementation;
  • interoperability of AIKOM’s school and teacher identifiers with other systems cannot be assumed (see Annex 3, Section B.1, Data linkage).

The Client will provide or facilitate access to these sources at the start of the assignment. Primary data collection should be priced only for the evidence gaps identified in these Terms of Reference, not for reconstruction of administrative data.

These sources provide evidence on formal delivery but do not systematically establish actual use, changes in practice, or the reasons for variation in implementation across schools. The evaluation shall therefore complement and triangulate existing data to assess how the pilot is implemented in practice and to identify the implementation-related and structural or contextual factors associated with variation, including unresolved school-network arrangements.

Classroom teaching practices in the pilot schools are also measured under the parallel assignment LEARN-2.4-TEACH, which applies the Teach Secondary classroom observation tool). The process evaluation shall use relevant instruments and data from that assignment and avoid duplication (see Component 3).Because the Teach Secondary tool does not define track-specific expectations, it may not show whether teaching meets the requirements of the basic and advanced tracks; the Consultant shall therefore complement it with a supplementary track-specific observation module (see Annex 3, Section B.3)

The Consultant will be contracted in line with the World Bank Procurement Regulations. These Terms of Reference define the purpose, scope and duration of the consulting services and the qualification requirements for the Consultant.

 

III. SCOPE OF SERVICES

This section summarises what is procured, in what volume and in what form. The detailed methodological specification is set out in Annex 3, which forms an integral part of these Terms of Reference.  The five specific objectives and five key evaluation questions remain the governing framework, but the depth of analysis shall be differentiated: all eight evaluation thematic areas receive descriptive coverage, while the core questions and priority mechanisms identified in Annex 2 receive in-depth treatment. Exact sequencing and operational details may be refined in the Inception Report, subject to Client approval.

Summary of the services

The Client procures an independent process evaluation that consists of:

  • an inception package that turns the Theory of Change and the evaluation questions into an agreed evaluation matrix, methodology and set of instruments (Component 1);
  • a system-wide implementation profile of all 150 pilot schools, based mainly on existing data (Component 2);
  • primary data collection: two survey rounds, comparative case studies in 10 schools, 20 lesson observations and a limited number of key-informant interviews (Component 3);
  • a comparative analysis of implementation variation, mechanisms and assumptions (Component 4);
  • a synthesis with scale-up conditions and prioritised recommendations, an interim learning session and a final workshop (Component 5).

The services are delivered through four deliverables over up to eight months and a final data package (Section IV).

Evaluation framework

The evaluation covers four levels of the Theory of Change (Annex 1): (1) inputs, (2) delivery activities, (3) changes in practice and (4) intermediate outcomes (cross-cutting). It covers the following eight evaluation thematic areas:

  • legal and regulatory framework;
  • curriculum and student choice;
  • teacher development;
  • principal and school-leadership development;
  • content and materials;
  • infrastructure and resources;
  • governance, monitoring and coordination;
  • student and family experience.

Annex 2 provides guiding evaluation questions and identifies their priority and primary evidence level. The Consultant may refine or consolidate secondary questions during inception, subject to Client approval, provided that the five key evaluation questions, core questions and priority mechanisms remain covered.

Component 4. Comparative analysis of implementation variation, mechanisms and assumptions

The Consultant shall combine the 150-school profile with the primary evidence to explain why implementation succeeds or encounters difficulties under different conditions. The analysis shall in particular:

  • assess teacher development and school-leadership development as distinct but interacting pathways, and school management capacity as a cross-cutting mechanism;

  • analyse the implementation-support cascade, including the role of founders/hromadas and of the coordination mechanisms;

Detailed requirements: Annex 3, Section B.4.

Component 5. Synthesis, scale-up recommendations and knowledge transfer

The Consultant shall integrate all evidence into a coherent assessment of implementation and its implications for the national scale-up, including:

  • a clear answer to each of the five key evaluation questions and specific objectives;
  • a classification of scale-up conditions into essential enabling conditions, constraints that can be compensated through additional support or adaptation, and structural limits to the current model;
  • identification of the components that can be scaled as designed, require modification or require differentiated approaches by context;
  • prioritised recommendations addressed to national bodies, oblast/regional actors, founders/hromadas and schools;
  • a limited set of priority indicators and data sources for monitoring after the evaluation, with suggested owners and frequency;
  • an interim learning session and a final dissemination/decision workshop with the Client and key stakeholders.

Detailed requirements: Annex 3, Section B.5.

Scope boundaries

The assignment is a process/implementation evaluation. It shall be designed to maximise decision value within the available time and financial envelope, using existing data for full-cohort coverage and concentrating resource-intensive fieldwork on analytically selected cases.

The following activities are outside the mandatory scope:

  • a stand-alone causal impact evaluation using a non-pilot control group, matching or difference-in-differences;
  • design and implementation of a separate diagnostic assessment of student learning outcomes;
  • redevelopment of the reform Theory of Change from first principles;
  • comprehensive in-person fieldwork in all 150 pilot schools;
  • creation of a permanent public dashboard or web platform for monitoring;
  • longitudinal tracking beyond the contract period.

The Consultant may, at no additional cost, undertake limited analysis of learning-outcome, diagnostic or comparison data generated by parallel initiatives if such data are readily available and directly relevant to the evaluation questions. This analysis is optional, shall not require additional primary data collection, and is not an expected deliverable.

The methodology, sampling design, fieldwork plan and staffing proposed by the Consultant shall be feasible within the maximum contract value specified in the procurement documents. The Consultant shall demonstrate the corresponding level of effort and allocation of resources in its technical proposal. Any material expansion of the agreed scope shall require prior written approval by the Client and, where applicable, a contract amendment.

Annex 3. Detailed Methodological Requirements

This Annex sets out the detailed methodological requirements for the services summarised in Section III. It forms an integral part of these Terms of Reference.

A. Minimum methodological requirements

The Consultant may propose the detailed design and analytical methods, but the methodology shall, at minimum:

  1. Be explicitly grounded in the agreed Theory of Change, five specific objectives, five key evaluation questions and the priority classification in Annex 2, applying lighter descriptive treatment to secondary questions and in-depth analysis to core questions and priority mechanisms.
  2. Use a mixed-methods approach combining quantitative, qualitative, administrative, documentary and direct-observation evidence.
  3. Prioritise audit, reuse and linkage of existing data before introducing new reporting requirements for schools.
  4. Triangulate self-report with independent documentary, administrative or observational evidence wherever reasonably possible.
  5. Distinguish formal delivery from verified receipt, usability/functionality and actual use.
  6. Assess both implementation fidelity and legitimate local adaptation.
  7. Analyse heterogeneity and implementation variation rather than relying only on pilot-wide averages.
  8. Examine the relative role of structural, contextual and wartime constraints and of implementation practices and management decisions in explaining variation, without making attribution claims that the design cannot support.
  9. Assess teacher development and school-leadership development separately as well as their interaction.
  10. Treat school leadership/management capacity as a construct requiring direct evidence, not as a simple proxy based on prior piloting or training attendance.
  11. Use purposive comparative sampling for qualitative case studies, informed by the implementation-variation dimensions (Section C) and updated implementation evidence.
  12. Apply appropriate statistical analysis to quantitative data and transparent thematic coding to qualitative evidence.
  13. Use contribution analysis and/or process tracing for priority mechanisms where these approaches add explanatory value.
  14. Include a transparent account of data quality, missingness, response rates, limitations, uncertainty and contradictions in the evidence.
  15. Produce reproducible and well-documented datasets, coding frameworks, indicator definitions and analysis scripts to the extent technically feasible.

B. Methodological specification by component

B.1. Inception and operationalisation of the evaluation framework (Component 1)

The Consultant shall:

  • Operationalise the ToC into an evaluation matrix linking objectives, evaluation questions, ToC levels, evaluation thematic areas, indicators or evidence criteria, data sources, analytical methods and deliverables.
  • Establish clear working definitions for implementation fidelity, reach, receipt, usability, use, adaptation, enabling conditions, compensable constraints, structural limits and early intermediate outcomes.
  • Conduct a rapid data audit covering ownership, coverage, identifiers, update frequency, completeness, quality, comparability and linkability of available administrative and monitoring sources.
  • Confirm and separately map the teacher-development and school-leadership/management-development pathways, including training-track coverage and participant-to-school linkage.
  • Identify evidence gaps requiring primary data collection and avoid duplicating information already available through administrative systems, existing monitoring or partner-generated data.
  • Develop a detailed mixed-methods methodology, analytical plan, fieldwork schedule and integration strategy for quantitative, qualitative, administrative and observational evidence.
  •  Develop a purposive sampling strategy for 10 comparative case studies, including selection criteria based on the implementation-variation dimensions in Section C. The final selection of case-study schools shall be confirmed in Deliverable D2 based on the available implementation evidence.
  • Finalise and pilot all required data-collection instruments, including survey instruments, interview/focus-group guides, document-review templates and classroom-observation protocols.
  • Prepare data-management, safeguarding, consent, research-ethics, security and remote-fieldwork procedures.
  • Conduct an inception workshop with the Client to confirm the evaluation matrix, samples, instruments, fieldwork approach, timeline, roles and risk-management arrangements.

Data linkage. Where source systems do not contain compatible identifiers, the Consultant shall quantify the achievable linkage coverage, document the resulting analytical limitations and propose feasible remedies. Creation of new cross-system identifiers or retrospective reconstruction of missing linkages is outside the mandatory scope unless separately agreed with the Client.

B.2. System-wide assessment of delivery, reach and use (Component 2)

The Consultant shall create a system-wide implementation profile for all 150 pilot schools using existing administrative, monitoring, documentary and survey evidence. The profile shall support descriptive analysis, disaggregation, identification of implementation patterns and selection of contrasting cases for deeper qualitative analysis.

The profile shall cover, as a minimum, the following aspects of each evaluation thematic area:

  1. Legal and regulatory framework: receipt and usability of the legal/regulatory conditions; notification of schools and founders; admission guidance; translation of national requirements into school- and community-level arrangements.
  2. Curriculum and student choice: alignment of curricula with selected tracks; opening of declared profiles and electives; organisation of profile choice, revisability, grouping and timetabling; alignment between declared and delivered offers.
  3. Teacher development: availability and timing of subject-relevant PD; reach of Vector/other approved programmes; operation and adequacy of money-follows-the-teacher virtual accounts; linkage between trained teachers and the subjects/grades they actually teach; application of competency-based and differentiated approaches.
  4. Principal and school-leadership development: management-track PD inputs and completion; participant-to-school linkage; leadership organisation of profiles, timetables, staffing and communication; problem solving; capacity planning; career-guidance arrangements; use of external expertise.
  5. Content and materials: availability and timing of new programmes and teaching/learning materials, taking account of the applicable approbation and textbook-production cycle; UIED approbation and textbook-piloting coverage; actual use in lessons; speed and usefulness of the feedback loop; school/teacher coping strategies where materials are missing or delayed.
  6. Infrastructure and resources: subventions and other financing; staffing for specialised hours; psychologist/social-pedagogue functions; equipment delivery, installation, functionality and use; learning spaces, connectivity, power, shelter, transport and boarding/accommodation where relevant.
  7. Governance, monitoring and coordination: functioning of NUS Implementation Office and other recurring coordination mechanisms; logging of requests, barriers, decisions and follow-up; data flows; escalation pathways; founder/hromada obligations and problem-solving role; whether evidence feeds into implementation adjustments.
  8. Student and family experience: timeliness and clarity of information; orientation, pre-specialisation and counselling; perceived reality and fairness of profile choice and admission; experience of school transition, longer travel or new routines; access barriers and groups most affected.

Wherever data permit, the Consultant shall distinguish what was planned or formally provided, what was received, what was operational or usable, and what was actually used. Structural or contextual variables shall not be collapsed into a simple performance or fidelity score unless the Consultant demonstrates a valid measurement approach and obtains Client approval.

B.3. Primary stakeholder research and direct verification (Component 3)

The Consultant shall collect primary evidence sufficient to verify implementation and explain stakeholder experience where administrative reporting is incomplete or cannot establish actual use or practice. Primary data collection shall complement, not duplicate, existing monitoring.

Quantitative stakeholder research. The Consultant shall implement an early implementation survey round and a follow-up survey round during the contract period, aligned with the school calendar and contract start date.

  • School administration: seek coverage of all 150 pilot schools, with a concise instrument focused on implementation, leadership, staffing, profiles, resources, governance and local constraints.
  • Teachers: use two repeated cross-sectional survey rounds with a statistically and operationally adequate sample across the pilot cohort. The design shall support no more than three priority disaggregation dimensions agreed at inception. It is not required to support statistically powered estimates for every intersection of these dimensions.
  • Students: use two repeated cross-sectional survey rounds with a statistically and operationally adequate sample across the pilot cohort, focused on profile choice, access, course delivery, learning experience, safety, support and transition. The design shall support no more than three priority disaggregation dimensions agreed at inception. It is not required to support statistically powered estimates for every intersection of these dimensions.
  • Parents/caregivers: conduct one round with a targeted quantitative sample to answer questions on information, admission, choice, transition, transport/access and family experience; a full census is not required.
  • Founders/community representatives: conduct one targeted structured data-collection round focused on financing, network decisions, transport/boarding, administrative support and founder-school interaction.
  • All questionnaires shall be concise, role-specific and explicitly mapped to the evaluation matrix. The Consultant shall justify sample sizes, response-rate targets, non-response procedures and any weighting strategy in the Inception Report.

School administration shall use a panel (linked) design across the two rounds where feasible. Teacher and student surveys shall use repeated cross-sectional designs. Parents/caregivers and founders shall be covered in one round. The Inception Report shall also define the interval between rounds, the analytical interpretation of change between rounds and, for school administration only where a panel is used, respondent-linkage and attrition procedures.

 

Comparative qualitative case studies.  The Consultant shall conduct in-depth comparative case studies in 10 pilot schools selected purposively to represent contrasting implementation contexts. The sampling approach and selection criteria shall be approved at inception, and the final case-study sample shall be confirmed in Deliverable D2 based on early implementation evidence. Replacing a case after fieldwork has started shall be treated as a scope change and require prior Client approval. Any follow-up after the main case-study fieldwork shall be remote and limited to up to five case-study schools; additional in-person visits are outside the mandatory scope unless separately agreed. The technical proposal shall state the planned number of field days per case-study school.

 

  • Semi-structured interviews with school leaders and relevant leadership-team members.
  • Interviews with representatives of founders/hromadas and, where analytically relevant, oblast or other implementation-support actors.
  • Teacher and student focus groups and/or qualitative interviews in a purposive subset of case-study schools.
  • Targeted parent/caregiver interviews or focus groups only in case-study schools where family experience is directly relevant to understanding information, choice, transition, commuting or access barriers.
  • Document review and verification of local implementation arrangements, including profile offer, curricula/timetables, staffing, admission, career guidance, resource use and local decisions.
  • Where feasible and safe, school walkthroughs and direct verification of implementation conditions directly relevant to the selected case, including learning environments, equipment, or transport/boarding arrangements where applicable.

Classroom observation. The Consultant shall use direct lesson/classroom observation to assess whether intended teaching and assessment practices are visible in practice and whether specialised materials, spaces and equipment are being used. The Consultant shall propose the observation approach (existing TEACH instruments complemented by the supplementary track-specific module described below), observer-training procedure and quality-control approach. Indicatively, the assignment should include approximately 20 lesson observations across at least five case-study schools and a range of profiles/subjects, with exact numbers finalised at inception.

Classroom observations are intended as comparative case-study and mechanism-verification evidence and shall not be treated as statistically representative of teaching practice across the full 150-school pilot.

The Consultant shall review relevant existing observation instruments and datasets generated under parallel initiatives, including LEARN-2.4-TEACH, and shall use or adapt them where methodologically appropriate. Because the Teach Secondary tool does not define track-specific expectations, the Consultant shall develop a concise supplementary observation module that operationalises the intended competency-based and differentiated teaching practices for the basic and advanced tracks, based on the State Standard of profile secondary education and the relevant curricula. The criteria shall be agreed with the Client at inception. A full stand-alone observation protocol is not required.

 

Governance and implementation-support interviews. To assess the support cascade and governance pathway, the Consultant shall conduct a limited purposive set of key-informant interviews with relevant national implementation actors and selected oblast/subnational actors only where directly relevant to a priority mechanism or case study. The interviews shall clarify how coordination, data flows, escalation, decision-making and follow-up operate in practice, including the respective roles of MoES/NUS Implementation Office, oblast-level actors, founders/hromadas and schools. Up to three interviews with relevant teacher-training providers may be included to assess teacher-development delivery and the money-follows-the-teacher mechanism. The sample shall be finalised at inception.

Triangulation. All primary evidence shall be triangulated across respondent groups and against administrative, documentary and observational evidence wherever feasible. Self-report alone shall not be treated as sufficient verification when an independent source is reasonably available.

B.4. Comparative analysis of implementation variation, mechanisms and assumptions (Component 4)

The Consultant shall conduct theory-based comparative analysis of contrasting cases to explain why implementation succeeds or encounters difficulties under different conditions. The analysis shall combine the 150-school system-wide profile with primary evidence from case studies and direct verification.

  • Compare schools with varying levels of relevant enabling conditions to identify factors that consistently distinguish stronger from weaker implementation, while avoiding causal claims not supported by the design.
  • Assess teacher development and principal/school-leadership development as distinct pathways and examine how they interact at school level.
  • Examine school leadership/management capacity as a cross-cutting mechanism rather than treating training completion as a proxy for capacity.
  • Prioritise in-depth testing of the four priority mechanisms defined in Section II: the functioning of money-follows-the-teacher, school management capacitythe adequacy and use of management-track PD, and the speed and usefulness of the materials-approbation feedback loop.
  • Analyse the implementation-support cascade and identify where bottlenecks are flagged, escalated and resolved; whether schools rely first on founders/hromadas or bypass them; and whether recurring coordination produces concrete decisions that reach school leaders and teachers in a timely way.
  • Distinguish implementation-fidelity problems, structural/contextual constraints, legitimate adaptations that preserve core reform intent, adaptations that materially weaken or alter the model, and design assumptions requiring system-level revision.
  • Use contribution analysis and/or process tracing, where appropriate, to test whether the expected mechanism is supported by the sequence and triangulation of available evidence and to consider plausible alternative explanations.

B.5. Synthesis, scale-up recommendations and knowledge transfer (Component 5)

The Consultant shall synthesise quantitative, qualitative, administrative, documentary and observational evidence into a coherent assessment of implementation and its implications for national scale-up.

  • Provide a clear answer to each of the five key evaluation questions and specific objectives.
  • Identify what is working as intended, what is not, where the implementation chain breaks, and which adaptations appear effective.
  • Classify relevant scale-up conditions into: (i) essential enabling conditions; (ii) constraints that can be compensated through additional support or adaptation; and (iii) structural limits to the current model.
  • Specify which components can be scaled as designed, which require modification, and which require differentiated implementation approaches by context.
  • Differentiate recommendations by responsibility: national policy/implementation bodies, oblast/regional actors where relevant, founders/hromadas, and schools.
  • Prioritise recommendations by urgency and importance and identify actions required before and during national rollout.
  • Identify a limited set of priority indicators and data sources that should continue to be monitored after the evaluation, with suggested owners and frequency.
  • Present and discuss findings with the Client and key stakeholders through an interim learning session and a final dissemination/decision workshop.

C. Indicative implementation-variation dimensions

The qualitative case-study sample should consider the following dimensions where analytically relevant. Quantitative disaggregation shall be limited to no more than three of these dimensions, agreed at inception.These variables are intended to support explanation and case selection, not to create a simple school ranking:

  • previous participation in the upper-secondary pre-pilot and/or earlier NUS piloting;
  • school leadership and management readiness/capacity;
  • urban, rural and mountainous contexts;
  • actual cohort size and cohort stability between selection and the school year;
  • number and diversity of profiles and clusters offered;
  • only-lyceum versus multiple-lyceum community contexts;
  • school structure (e.g., upper-secondary-only versus broader grade spans);
  • in-person, blended and distance-learning modalities, including displacement and security conditions;
  • boarding, transport and physical accessibility;
  • staffing capacity and student-teacher ratios;
  • infrastructure, equipment, connectivity, shelter capacity and actual use of learning environments;
  • local fiscal/economic capacity;
  • language of instruction or other specific implementation contexts;
  • participation in materials/textbook testing or approbation and availability of profile-relevant materials.

D. Research-ethics and data-protection protocol

The research-ethics and data-protection protocol referred to in Section VI shall address, at minimum:

  • informed consent and, where applicable, parental/guardian consent and student assent;
  • voluntary participation and the right to withdraw;
  • age-appropriate communication and safeguarding procedures for minors;
  • minimisation of collection of personally identifiable information and sensitive data;
  • anonymisation/de-identification and separation of identifiers from analytical datasets;
  • complete deletion of non-anonymous raw data;
  • secure data transfer, storage and hosting arrangements; roles and responsibilities for data control and processing; access control and access logging; conditions for any cross-border data transfer; controls applicable to subcontractors and subprocessors; security-incident and breach-notification procedures; implementation of the least access principle during storage and transfer procedures;and data-retention and secure-deletion procedures;
  • procedures for reporting findings so that individuals cannot be re-identified;
  • Security protocols for fieldwork in conflict-affected settings and remote research where relevant;
  • compliance with applicable Ukrainian legislation, GDPR, and any additional requirements established by the Client or funder.

 

[1] Subject domains supported by the NUS reform: Ukrainian language and literature, Mathematics, Natural Sciences, Technology, Informatics, Social and Health Education, Civics and History, Arts, and Physical Education.

CONSULTING SERVICES FOR THE DEVELOPMENT OF DRAFT STATUTORY INSTRUMENTS AND GUIDELINES TO ENHANCE PROTECTION, MANAGEMENT, COLLABORATION AND ECONOMIES OF NATURAL RESOURCES IN PROTECTED AREAS AND NATIONAL HERITAGE.

Country:

CONSULTING SERVICES FOR THE DEVELOPMENT OF DRAFT STATUTORY INSTRUMENTS AND GUIDELINES TO ENHANCE PROTECTION, MANAGEMENT, COLLABORATION AND ECONOMIES OF NATURAL RESOURCES IN PROTECTED AREAS AND NATIONAL HERITAGE.

Introduction

The Government of the Republic of Zambia (GRZ) has received financing from the World Bank toward the cost of the Zambia Green, Resilient and Transformational Tourism Development Project (GREAT-TDP) and intends to apply part of the proceeds for consulting services.

The Ministry of Tourism (MoT), through the Green, Resilient and Transformational Tourism Development Project (GREAT-TDP), intends to engage a qualified consulting firm or consortium of firms to support the development of draft Statutory Instruments (SIs) and operational Guidelines aimed at strengthening the regulatory framework governing protected areas, wildlife resources, and natural heritage sites in Zambia, including operational interfaces with forest areas where these overlap with protected areas or heritage sites.

The assignment forms part of Task 1.2.2: Concession Frameworks and Collaborative Management Partnerships Across Landscapes under Component 1 of the GREAT-TDP. The consultancy seeks to establish a functional regulatory framework that promotes sustainable conservation, enhances private sector participation, supports community engagement, and facilitates nature-based investments in protected landscapes.

The Ministry of Tourism, through the Project Implementation Unit (PIU), now invites eligible consulting firms to indicate their interest in providing these services. Interested firms may associate with other firms in the form of a Joint Venture, Consortium, or Sub-consultancy arrangement to enhance their qualifications.

Scope of the Assignment

The consultancy will include, but not be limited to, the following:

  • Review and analysis of existing legislation, policies, regulations, statutory instruments, and guidelines governing wildlife, protected areas, heritage conservation, tourism concessions, and related sectors, including forest-related frameworks only to the extent necessary to address operational overlaps with protected areas and heritage sites;
  • Identification of regulatory gaps, overlaps, inconsistencies, and barriers affecting conservation and private sector participation;
  • Stakeholder consultations with government institutions, local communities, traditional leaders, private sector actors, civil society organizations, conservation partners, and development partners;
  • Drafting and refinement, through a phased and prioritized process, of the Statutory Instruments and Guidelines identified in the Terms of Reference, currently comprising approximately twenty (20) instruments under the Wildlife and Protected Areas framework and the National Heritage Conservation Commission Act, together with agreed joint operational procedures addressing interfaces with forest areas. Forest Act reform and standalone forestry subsidiary legislation are outside the scope of this assignment;
  • Development of legal and operational frameworks for tourism concessions, collaborative management partnerships, community participation, wildlife management, carbon trading, biodiversity credits, and sustainable natural resource utilization, subject to the assignment boundaries set out in the Terms of Reference;
  • Development of training materials and delivery of Training of Trainers (ToT) programmes to support implementation of the new regulatory framework;
  • Development of communication materials to support awareness and dissemination of the new regulatory instruments; and
  • Provision of recommendations to strengthen inter-agency coordination and management of overlapping land-use interests across protected landscapes.

The assignment is expected to be implemented over a period of approximately eighteen (18) months.

Eligibility and Submission of Expressions of Interest

Interested consulting firms should provide information demonstrating that they possess the required qualifications and relevant experience to perform the services.

The Expression of Interest should include:

  • Cover letter expressing interest in undertaking the assignment;
  • Company profile, including legal status, ownership structure, and areas of specialization;
  • Evidence of experience in similar assignments, particularly in legal drafting, policy and regulatory reform, protected area governance, wildlife conservation, forestry, heritage conservation, natural resource management, and public-private partnership frameworks;
  • Details of at least five (5) similar assignments successfully completed within the last ten (10) years, including client references;
  • Demonstration of experience in Zambia and/or Sub-Saharan Africa in natural resource governance and regulatory reform;
  • Description of technical and managerial capacity of the firm;
  • Contact details including physical address, telephone number, and email address.

Shortlisting Criteria

The shortlist shall be established based on the following criteria:

  1. Core Business and Experience: At least 10 years of experience in providing legal, policy, regulatory, and institutional advisory services.
  2. Relevant Similar Experience: Successful completion of at least five (5) similar assignments within the last 10 years involving the drafting, review, or reform of legislation, regulations, policies, guidelines, or institutional frameworks in wildlife, forestry, tourism, heritage, environmental governance, natural resource management, or related sectors. Experience in Zambia, Sub-Saharan Africa, or comparable jurisdictions will be an added advantage.
  3. Technical and Managerial Capacity: Demonstrated organizational, technical, and project management capacity to successfully deliver assignments of comparable scope and complexity. (Key Experts will not be evaluated at the shortlisting stage. Shortlisting will be based solely on the qualifications and experience of consulting firms. The qualifications of proposed experts will be assessed during the proposal evaluation stage).
  4. Stakeholder Engagement Experience: Demonstrated experience in conducting stakeholder consultations and supporting policy, legal, and institutional reform processes involving public and private sector stakeholders.

The attention of interested Consultants is drawn to Paragraph 3.14 of the World Bank Procurement Regulations for IPF Borrowers, September 2025 (Seventh Edition), setting forth the World Bank’s policy on Conflict of Interest.

A Consultant will be selected in accordance with the Quality and Cost-Based Selection (QCBS) method set out in the World Bank Procurement Regulations for IPF Borrowers.

REQUEST FOR EXPRESSIONS OF INTEREST

(INDIVIDUAL CONSULTING SERVICES)

Syrian Arab Republic

Syria Public Financial Management Capacity Strengthening Project (P512516)

Grant No.: E6410-SY

Assignment Title: SIFMIS Program Manager (Syria Integrated Financial Management Information System)

Reference No. (as per Procurement Plan): SY-MOF-583041-CS-INDV

The Ministry of Finance of the Syrian Arab Republic (the “Employer”) has received financing from the World Bank towards the cost of the Syria Public Financial Management Capacity Strengthening Project (P512516) and intends to apply part of the proceeds for consulting services.

The consulting services (“the Services”) include the services of a SIFMIS Program Manager, who will provide the Government of Syria with experienced, full-time program management leadership and functional advisory for the implementation of the Syria Integrated Financial Management Information System (SIFMIS), ensuring effective planning, coordination, quality assurance, risk management, vendor governance, and change management throughout the system's design, procurement, configuration, testing, rollout, and stabilization phases.

The SIFMIS Program Manager combines program management leadership with business analysis and functional expertise, reflecting the need for a single accountable leader who can govern the vendor relationship at both the program level and the functional process level, and who can effectively represent the Ministry of Finance's interests in reviewing and approving all functional deliverables produced by the implementation vendor. The SIFMIS Program Manager will lead program planning and management across the full SIFMIS lifecycle - requirements validation, design, configuration and development, data migration, integration, testing, training, rollout, and post-go-live support; review and recommend acceptance or rejection of the vendor's IT infrastructure assessment, technical architecture, network and security architecture, and data center readiness; lead the government-side functional engagement across all SIFMIS modules; support the RFP finalization, bid evaluation and contract negotiation; oversee data migration, User Acceptance Testing, change management and training; maintain the program risk register; and oversee the post-go-live stabilization and the capacity building of the Ministry of Finance's SIFMIS Reform Implementation Team (RIT). The assignment is expected to span approximately thirty-six (36) months, covering the diagnostic and design, procurement support, and implementation oversight and capacity building phases.

The SIFMIS Program Manager will report to the Project Coordinator and will work within the Public Financial Management Reform Coordinating Unit (PFMRCU) of the Ministry of Finance, coordinating with the Ministry of Administrative Development (MoAD), line ministries, the Central Bank of Syria, the Supreme Audit Institution, the National Authority for IT Services (NAITS) and development partners, and reporting to the PFM Reform Oversight Steering Committee (PFM-ROSC) on overall program progress.

The detailed Terms of Reference (TOR) for the assignment are included below.

The Ministry of Finance (through the Public Financial Management Reform Coordinating Unit - PFMRCU) now invites eligible individuals (“Consultants”) to indicate their interest in providing the Services. Interested Consultants should provide information demonstrating that they have the required qualifications and relevant experience to perform the Services (attach curriculum vitae with description of experience in similar assignments, similar conditions, etc.). Firms' staff may express interest through the employing firm for the assignment and, under such situation, only the experience and qualifications of individuals shall be considered in the selection process.

The criteria for selecting the Consultant are:

  1. an advanced degree (Master's level or equivalent) in Public Financial Management, Information Systems, Finance, or a related field, and a minimum of fifteen (15) years of professional experience in government IFMIS programs, with a career trajectory that includes hands-on functional or business analysis roles in earlier years and senior program management responsibility in later years;
  2. demonstrated experience as a functional lead or business analyst on at least two (2) IFMIS implementations - covering module design, business process validation, User Acceptance Testing (UAT) and training - before progressing to program management;
  3. demonstrated experience managing at least two (2) IFMIS implementation programs in developing or post-conflict country contexts at senior level;

Terms of Reference

SIFMIS Program Manager

Syria Integrated Financial Management Information System (SIFMIS)

1. Background and Context

The Government of the Syrian Arab Republic (GoS) is committed to rebuilding and modernizing its Public Financial Management (PFM) system as part of broader post-conflict reconstruction and institutional reform efforts. The Ministry of Finance (MoF) recognizes that a well-functioning Syria Integrated Financial Management Information System (SIFMIS) is essential to achieving transparent, accountable, and efficient management of public resources.

Strong government ownership, robust program management, and a pragmatic approach to implementation are critical success factors. The Syria Public Financial Management Capacity Strengthening Project (P512516) will finance the purchase, installation, integration, testing, user training, and commissioning of the SIFMIS, associated end-user devices, hardware, network infrastructure, and related support services. The envisaged Commercial Off-the-Shelf (COTS) SIFMIS will support procedural and control systems to ensure the legality, accuracy, and timeliness of fiscal information across core PFM functions including: budget preparation, budget execution, human resource and payroll management with biometric registration, expenditure control, cash management, purchasing, revenue management, fixed asset registration, inventory management, accounting, reporting, audit trails, and financial reporting and analytics.

The SIFMIS will include a seamlessly integrated centralized payroll module with biometric registration functionalities to enforce system-based entry/exit controls, position controls, grade/scale, location, and allowances. The payroll module will enhance the efficiency of human resource management (HRM) transactions under the control of the Ministry of Administrative Development (MoAD), enable the creation of a consolidated and up-to-date database of public sector employees, and facilitate reconciliation of personnel and payroll records.

The project will also finance the upgrade of the current Data Center at the MoF to meet data center functionality, capacity, uptime, and cybersecurity standards. SIFMIS connectivity will be through the Government Secure Network (GSN) managed by the National Authority for IT Services (NAITS).

Eight of the fifteen Governorate Finance Offices — Ministry of Finance (Central Department), Damascus, Damascus Rural, Aleppo, Tartous, Lattakia, Homs, and Hama — will be prioritized for the initial SIFMIS rollout, accounting for approximately eighty percent of average payment values. A rollout strategy will be developed to achieve full governorate coverage in the medium-term.

The State and Peace-Building Fund (SPF) has provided technical assistance to advance the Budget Classification and Chart of Accounts (BC-CoA) reform and develop functional requirements for the SIFMIS. These outputs provide the foundation for this assignment.

2. Objectives of the Assignment

The overall objective of this assignment is to provide the Government of Syria with experienced, full-time program management leadership and functional advisory for the implementation of the SIFMIS, ensuring effective planning, coordination, quality assurance, risk management, vendor governance, and change management throughout the system's design, procurement, configuration, testing, rollout, and stabilization phases.

The SIFMIS Program Manager combines program management leadership with business analysis and functional expertise, reflecting the need for a single accountable leader who can govern the vendor relationship at both the program level and the functional process level, and who can effectively represent MoF's interests in reviewing and approving all functional deliverables produced by the implementation vendor.

3. Scope of Work

The SIFMIS Program Manager will report to the Project Coordinator and will be responsible for the following:

3.1 Program Planning and Management

The SIFMIS Program Manager will develop and maintain a detailed program implementation plan covering all phases of the SIFMIS lifecycle — requirements validation, design, configuration and development, data migration, integration, testing, training, rollout, and post-go-live support. The Program Manager will track progress against agreed milestones, deliverables, and the overall project budget, escalating deviations and proposing corrective actions as needed.

3.2 IT Infrastructure Assessment Review

The IT Infrastructure Assessment is a vendor contractual deliverable. The SFMIS Manager will review, challenge, and recommend acceptance or rejection of the vendor's assessment, covering:

    • Hardware, server capacity, and network connectivity at the PDC and across governorate sites
    • Existing software systems and integration interfaces
    • Cybersecurity and data protection arrangements
    • IT staffing capacity at MoF
    • GSN connectivity reliability and bandwidth by site

The SFMIS Manager will verify that the vendor's assessment is complete, accurate, and consistent with observed conditions at MoF facilities, and will produce a written review recommendation to the Project Coordinator before the assessment is formally accepted as a Phase 1 gateway document.

3.2 Technical Architecture Review

The SFMIS Manager will review and provide an independent technical assessment of the implementation vendor's proposed system architecture, covering:

    • Primary Data Center and Disaster Recovery Center design
    • Server topology, virtualization, and clustering configuration
    • Network segmentation, VLAN design, and firewall architecture
    • Offline and disconnected operations design
    • Backup and restoration architecture
    • Alignment with the outcome-based infrastructure requirements defined in the RFP

The SFMIS Manager  will recommend acceptance or rejection of the vendor's architecture to the Project Coordinator, with clear technical justification for the recommendation.

3.3 Business Process Review and Functional Advisory

Drawing on prior experience in PFM business analysis, business process re-imagination, and functional IFMIS design, the SIFMIS Program Manager will lead the government-side functional engagement with the implementation vendor across all SIFMIS modules, including:

    • Budget preparation and execution
    • Commitment control and payment processing
    • Treasury operations including cash and debt management
    • Accounting and financial reporting
    • Payroll and Human Resources management
    • Procurement and contract management
    • Revenue management and interfaces
    • Fixed asset and inventory management

The Program Manager will validate and challenge the vendor's business process and functional design documents against the SIFMIS RFP specifications, PFM legal and regulatory requirements, and international good practice (IPSAS cash basis, GFS 2014 classification). The Program Manager will recommend acceptance or rejection of all functional deliverables to the MoF and will ensure that the RIT is engaged and building capability throughout this process.

3.4 Network and Security Architecture Oversight

The SFMIS Manager will review and recommend acceptance or rejection of the vendor's Network Segmentation Design and Security Architecture Document — both of which are mandatory Phase 1 deliverables under the implementation contract. This includes:

    • Verification of network zone definitions, inter-zone traffic rules, and VLAN assignments
    • Assessment of firewall, IDS/IPS, and network monitoring configurations
    • Verification of encryption standards — AES-256 at rest, TLS 1.2 minimum in transit
    • Review of penetration testing plan and vulnerability disclosure procedures
    • Assessment of vendor remote access controls and session monitoring
    • Sign-off recommendation to the SIFMIS Program Manager before any network installation begins

3.5 Data Center Readiness

The SFMIS Manager will independently verify that the PDC refurbishment meets the requirements specified in the implementation contract before hardware delivery and installation is authorized. This includes physical inspection of rack installation, power feeds, UPS, generator, cooling, and physical security. The Technical Lead will issue a formal Data Center Readiness sign-off recommendation before hardware delivery proceeds.

3.6 Procurement Support

The SIFMIS Program Manager will support the Project Procurement Officer in finalizing the RFP documentation for the SIFMIS procurement, building on the functional and technical specifications already developed under the SPF grant. This includes supporting the Bidders' Conference, responding to vendor inquiries, supporting the evaluation panel in assessing proposals and determining evaluation scores, and assisting with contract negotiations and finalization of the implementation plan and timetable.

The Program Manager will advise the evaluation panel on the functional and programmatic merits of proposals but will not act as a sole decision-maker on vendor selection. Final scoring and selection authority rests with the MoF-appointed evaluation panel.

3.7 Vendor and Contract Management

The SIFMIS Program Manager will serve as the primary government-side counterpart to the implementation vendor for all program and functional matters. Responsibilities include:

    • Reviewing and recommending acceptance or rejection of vendor deliverables against RFP specifications
    • Monitoring vendor performance against contractual milestones and service level agreements
    • Managing contract variations, change requests, and scope disputes in coordination with MoF procurement and legal advisors
    • Certifying functional milestone completion as a condition for vendor payment
    • Escalating unresolved issues to the PFM Reform Oversight Steering Committee (PFM-ROSC)

Technical deliverable review — covering system architecture, infrastructure, network, security, and integration — will be led by the SIFMIS Technical Lead, working under the Program Manager's overall direction.

3.8 Stakeholder Coordination

The SIFMIS Program Manager will coordinate across the Ministry of Finance, MoAD, line ministries, the Central Bank, the Supreme Audit Institution, NAITS, and development partners, ensuring that functional requirements, business process changes, and implementation timelines are aligned and communicated effectively. The Program Manager will chair or co-chair working-level coordination meetings and prepare steering committee papers for PFM-ROSC review.

3.9 Data Migration Oversight

The SIFMIS Program Manager will oversee and challenge the vendor's data migration strategy from a functional perspective, ensuring that BC-CoA migration, opening balance migration, payroll data migration, and supplier master data migration are aligned with MoF requirements and that acceptance criteria are defined and met before production data loads are approved. The Program Manager will work closely with the SIFMIS Technical Lead on migration execution and data integrity validation.

3.10 Testing and User Acceptance

The SIFMIS Program Manager will lead the government-side oversight of User Acceptance Testing (UAT), reviewing the vendor's test scripts for functional completeness, facilitating RIT participation in UAT execution, reviewing defect logs, and recommending go-live approval or rejection based on UAT outcomes. The Program Manager will ensure that UAT is conducted against agreed functional acceptance criteria and that no critical defects remain open at go-live.

3.11 Change Management, Training, and Communication

The SIFMIS Program Manager will oversee the design and delivery of the change management and communication strategy, including the training-of-trainers program and end-user training plan. The Program Manager will review and recommend acceptance of all training materials produced by the vendor, ensure materials are available in Arabic and English before training commences, and verify that adequate user support arrangements — help desk, super-user network — are established and operational before go-live.

3.12 Risk Management and Reporting

The SIFMIS Program Manager will maintain a program risk register covering technical, institutional, capacity-related, and cybersecurity risks, and will prepare regular progress reports for the PFM-ROSC and the World Bank. Reports will cover milestone status, risk and issue status, vendor performance, financial progress, and recommended actions.

3.13 Post-Go-Live Stabilization

The SIFMIS Program Manager will oversee the hypercare and stabilization period following go-live, ensuring rapid resolution of production issues, coordinating between the vendor support team and MoF users, and supporting the transition of system ownership and maintenance responsibilities to the MoF SIFMIS support unit.

3.14 Capacity Building and Sustainability

The SIFMIS Program Manager will advise on the organizational structure and staffing requirements for the central SIFMIS support unit within the MoF and MoAD, including options for attracting and retaining qualified technical and functional staff given government salary constraints, and recommendations on in-sourcing versus outsourcing of specific functions. The Program Manager will actively build the capacity of RIT members throughout the assignment so that the government can increasingly own and direct the program over time.

4. Governance Deliverables

The SIFMIS Program Manager will produce the following governance outputs throughout the assignment. These are oversight and advisory outputs — not the technical or functional deliverables that the implementation vendor is contracted to produce. The vendor's deliverables are reviewed, challenged, and recommended for acceptance or rejection by the Program Manager; the outputs listed below are the Program Manager's own accountability to MoF.

5. Duration and Timing

The assignment is expected to span approximately 36 months, with the following indicative timeline:

  • Phase 1 — Diagnostic and Design: Months 1–6
  • Phase 2 — Procurement Support: Months 6–12
  • Phase 3 — Implementation Oversight and Capacity Building: Months 13–36

The SIFMIS Program Manager shall submit a detailed work plan with milestones within four weeks of contract signing. The timeline is indicative and may be adjusted based on the pace of government decisions, procurement processes, and vendor performance.

6. Institutional Arrangements

The Ministry of Finance, through the SIFMIS Reform Implementation Team (RIT), shall be the primary counterpart and focal point for coordination throughout the assignment. The MoF shall constitute a dedicated SIFMIS RIT comprising technical staff from relevant departments — Budget, Treasury, Accounting, Revenue, Payroll, and IT — to work alongside the Program Manager and build ownership of the program over time.

The PFM Reform Oversight Steering Committee (PFM-ROSC), comprising representatives from the Ministry of Finance, relevant line ministries, MoAD, and the Central Bank of Syria, is empowered to make key policy decisions, approve major deliverables including RFP release and vendor selection, and resolve implementation issues that cannot be resolved at the program level.

The MoF shall provide the Program Manager with office space in Damascus, furniture, and access to internet and telephone services, and all computing, printing, and presentation equipment required for the assignment.

7. Required Qualifications and Experience

This assignment requires an individual who has progressed from hands-on PFM business analysis and functional IFMIS implementation into senior program management and stakeholder coordination. Candidates who have only held project management roles without prior functional or business analysis experience in IFMIS implementations will not meet the profile for this role.

Required qualifications and experience:

  • Advanced degree (Master's level or equivalent) in Public Financial Management, Information Systems, Finance, or a related field
  • Minimum 15 years of professional experience in government IFMIS programs, with a career trajectory that includes hands-on functional or business analysis roles in earlier years and senior program management responsibility in later years
  • Demonstrated experience as a functional lead or business analyst on at least two IFMIS implementations — covering module design, business process validation, UAT, and training — before progressing to program management
  • Demonstrated experience managing at least two IFMIS implementation programs in developing or post-conflict country contexts at senior level
  • Deep knowledge of PFM processes across budget, treasury, payroll, procurement, and accounting functions, with ability to independently challenge and validate vendor functional designs
  • Knowledge of international PFM standards including GFS 2014, IPSAS cash basis, and PEFA assessment frameworks
  • Experience in developing or reviewing technical specifications and RFPs for government IFMIS procurement
  • Familiarity with World Bank Procurement Regulations for IPF Borrowers; experience managing procurement under World Bank-financed projects is a strong advantage
  • Demonstrated experience in capacity building, training oversight, and change management for government staff
  • Professional certification highly desirable: PMP, PRINCE2, or equivalent
  • Prior experience in fragile, conflict-affected, or post-conflict environments is highly desirable
  • Proficiency in English is required. Arabic language proficiency is a strong advantage given the need to work directly with Syrian government counterparts

8. Reporting Requirements

The SIFMIS Program Manager shall report to the Project Coordinator at the Ministry of Finance on day-to-day operational matters, and to the PFM-ROSC on overall program progress.

The Program Manager shall submit:

  • Monthly progress reports covering milestone status, issues encountered, risk register update, vendor performance summary, and planned activities for the following month
  • Deliverable review recommendations as listed in Section 5, with accept or reject recommendation and supporting justification
  • Steering committee papers for each PFM-ROSC meeting
  • A Final Completion Report summarizing assignment outcomes, lessons learned, and recommendations for the next phase of SIFMIS development

9. Ethical Standards and Conflict of Interest

The SIFMIS Program Manager shall disclose any actual or potential conflict of interest at the outset of the assignment and throughout its duration. The Program Manager shall not act as a decision-maker in the SIFMIS vendor selection process if they have any financial or commercial relationship with any bidding firm, and shall advise the MoF of any such relationship immediately upon becoming aware of it.

All work products, reports, and recommendations produced under this assignment shall remain the intellectual property of the Government of the Syrian Arab Republic. The Program Manager shall treat all government data, system architecture details, personnel records, fiscal information, and implementation details as strictly confidential and shall not disclose any such information to third parties during or after the assignment without explicit written authorization from the MoF.

10. Budget and Payment

The Program Manager's remuneration shall be based on a time-based contract, with payments linked to the satisfactory submission and acceptance of monthly progress reports and governance deliverables as specified in Section 5. The detailed payment schedule shall be agreed upon during contract negotiations.

REQUEST FOR EXPRESSIONS OF INTEREST

Country: Lebanon

Project Name: Digital Skilling for Employment (DSE) Project

Grant / Trust Fund Nos.: MDTF-FD Grant No. TF0D1059 & JSDF Grant No. TF0D1200

Assignment Title: Digital Trainer

STEP Activity Reference No.: 571859

 

1. Background & Context

The Digital Opportunity Trust (DOT Lebanon) has received financing from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (the World Bank), acting as administrator of the Japan Social Development Fund (JSDF Grant No. TF0D1200) and the Dutch PROSPECTS Fund (MDTF-FD Grant No. TF0D1059), toward the cost of the Digital Skilling for Employment (DSE) Project, and intends to apply part of the proceeds for consulting services.

 

The DSE Project aims to equip vulnerable youth and women across Lebanon with market-relevant digital skills and link them to real income-generating opportunities. Under Component 2: Productive Inclusion in the Digital Economy (Microwork)—specifically Subcomponent 2.2 (JSDF and PROSPECTS Package of Services for Microwork Inclusion)—DOT Lebanon provides digital, technical, and soft skills training paired with coaching, platform profile creation, and direct linkage to online microwork opportunities.

 

2. Objective & Scope of the Assignment

DOT Lebanon is seeking a qualified Individual Consultant to serve as Digital Trainer, reporting directly to the Area Manager. The Digital Trainer will deliver high-quality, inclusive, and market-relevant digital training programs for youth and adults across Lebanon, building the practical digital and employability-oriented skills participants need to engage in microwork, freelancing, and digital employment.

 

Key parameters and responsibilities of the assignment include:

 

  • Modular Training Delivery: Deliver structured, in-person training modules using DOT Lebanon-approved curricula, training materials, learning resources, and assessment tools across four thematic streams:
    • Technical Digital Skills: Data labeling, data collection, call center/customer service, Google tools, and graphic design.
    • Digital Safety: Cybersecurity and responsible online behavior.
    • Financial Literacy: Online payments, taxation, and income tracking.
    • Soft Skills: Communication, leadership, time management, critical thinking, self-marketing, and business ethics. (Trainers will be assigned to specific modules according to their qualifications and demonstrated expertise; one trainer is not expected to cover all technical, financial literacy, digital safety, and soft-skills topics.)
  • Cohort Structure & Geographic Coverage: The assignment covers 74 training groups in total (approximately 25 participants per group), distributed among 8 Digital Trainers across Lebanon according to the DSE implementation schedule. Under JSDF, each cohort receives 36 hours of training (12 sessions of 3 hours); under PROSPECTS, each cohort receives 72 hours of training (24 sessions of 3 hours).
  • Safeguarding & Field Coordination: Ensure a safe, inclusive learning environment in compliance with DOT Lebanon safeguarding, child protection, and Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) standards (including mandatory PSEA training and certification by the PSEA Focal Point), while coordinating closely with Area Managers and Field Officers on scheduling, logistics, and participant mobilization.
  • Documentation & Reporting: Maintain attendance records and session logs; administer and document approved pre- and post-assessments, assignments, and practical exercises; submit a monthly timesheet and invoice on the 25th of each month; and submit a cohort completion report upon completing each assigned cohort.
  • Duration & Level of Effort (LoE): The assignment will run from the date of contract signature until December 31, 2027. The Digital Trainer will be remunerated on an hourly basis at $20 per hour, subject to a maximum contract ceiling of $10,400 (an overall indicative LoE of up to approximately 520 total working hours, with an estimated monthly commitment of 15 to 40 hours per month depending on assigned cohort schedules).

The complete Terms of Reference (TOR) for the assignment is attached to this Request for Expressions of Interest.

 

3. Required Qualifications & Shortlisting Criteria

DOT Lebanon now invites eligible Individual Consultants ("Consultants") to indicate their interest in providing the Services. Interested Consultants must submit an updated Curriculum Vitae (CV) and supporting documentation demonstrating that they meet the following qualifications and evaluation criteria:

 

  1. Educational Requirements:
    • Bachelor's degree in Information Technology, Computer Science, Education, Instructional Design, Digital Media, Business Administration, Finance, Accounting, or a related field relevant to the assigned training module(s).
