The assignment falls under Component 2: Productive Inclusion in the Digital Economy (Microwork), which prepares vulnerable youth to participate in microwork opportunities through practical skills, mentorship, and access to freelance opportunities. DOT Lebanon is responsible for implementing Component 2.

Under Component 2, Subcomponent 2.1: Supply and Demand Assessment includes the assessment of youth baseline skills and constraints, local, regional, and global microwork demand, potential digital employment sectors, and clients and microwork platforms for partnership and micro-job creation. Subcomponent 2.2: JSDF and PROSPECTS Package of Services for Microwork Inclusion includes digital, technical and soft skills training, coaching and support to complete microtasks, profile creation on microwork platforms, and linkage to microwork opportunities.

 

  1. General Introduction & Grant Description: 

 

Lebanon continues to face one of the world’s most severe economic and financial crises, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Port of Beirut explosion, and the 2023-2024 conflict. These consecutive shocks have severely weakened labor market prospects, increased unemployment, and expanded poverty. Traditional employment pathways are increasingly constrained due to business closures, limited job creation, and instability.

 

At the same time, digital transformation and remote gig work are reshaping global labor markets. Microwork, small, simple digital tasks such as data tagging, transcription, verification, or AI data labeling, offers accessible, flexible income opportunities for individuals with basic digital literacy. Its low entry barriers make it particularly suitable for poor and vulnerable youth, women, and refugees.

 

The DSE project aims to equip youth and women with market-relevant digital skills and linking them to real income-generating opportunities, the Project supports Lebanon’s recovery from different crises while advancing WBG MENA strategies on human capital, economic inclusion, gender equality, and a resilient, future-ready workforce.

 

Under the DSE project, the Digital Skills for Employment (DSE) builds on global experiences in Economic Inclusion (EI) programs and adapts them to a digital context, replacing traditional asset transfers with tablets or smartphones and pairing skills training with coaching and direct linkage to online income opportunities.





 

  1. Objective and Scope of work: 

 

The Digital Trainers under the Digital Skills for Employment (DSE) Project are responsible for delivering high-quality, inclusive, and market-relevant digital training programs for youth and adults in Lebanon. Microwork is a central pathway under DSE, providing participants with an accessible entry point to online income-generating opportunities. The Digital Trainers contribute directly to this pathway by building the practical digital and employability-oriented skills participants need to engage in microwork, freelancing, and other digital employment opportunities.

 

The trainers will deliver assigned structured training modules covering technical digital skills (data labeling, data collection, call center/customer service, Google tools, and graphic design), soft skills (communication, leadership, time management, critical thinking, self-marketing, and business ethics), digital safety (cybersecurity and responsible online behavior), and financial literacy (online payments, taxation, and income tracking). DOT Lebanon will provide the approved curricula, training materials, learning resources, and assessment tools. Trainers are responsible for delivery and are not expected to develop or revise the curriculum or training content. They may adapt facilitation techniques and delivery methodologies to participants’ learning needs, but any substantive modification to the approved content requires prior approval from DOT Lebanon. Trainers will be assigned to modules according to their qualifications and demonstrated expertise; one trainer is not expected to cover the full range of technical, financial literacy, digital safety, and soft-skills topics.

 

The Digital Trainers will also ensure a safe and inclusive learning environment in line with DOT Lebanon safeguarding standards. They will be trained and certified on Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) by the PSEA Focal Point and are required to comply with all safeguarding, child protection, and ethical conduct policies. They will coordinate closely with Area Managers and Field Officers to ensure smooth implementation, participant engagement, and effective monitoring of training activities. The assignment covers 74 training groups in total, to be distributed among 8 Digital Trainers according to the DSE implementation schedule. Each group is expected to include approximately 25 participants. Under JSDF, each cohort receives 36 hours of training (12 sessions of 3 hours); under PROSPECTS, each cohort receives 72 hours of training (24 sessions of 3 hours). Training will be delivered in person across Lebanon. The training schedule will be coordinated between the relevant Area Manager, Trainer, and participants. The actual number of cohorts, sessions, beneficiaries, locations, and monthly assignments allocated to each trainer will be determined by DOT Lebanon based on implementation needs and reflected in the approved assignment schedule.

 

  1. Expected Deliverables and Reporting:

The Digital Trainer shall deliver assigned training sessions according to the agreed schedule and DOT Lebanon-approved curricula and materials; maintain attendance records; administer and document approved pre- and post-assessments, assignments, and practical exercises, as applicable; submit a timesheet monthly for payment purposes; and submit a simple cohort completion report upon completion of each assigned cohort.

The cohort completion report shall be submitted to the relevant Area Manager using a simple format provided or approved by DOT Lebanon and shall include, at a minimum, sessions delivered, attendance, assessment completion and results where applicable, key observations or challenges, and any required follow-up. Attendance records and session-level documentation shall be maintained and submitted in accordance with DOT Lebanon procedures.

  1. General Introduction & Grant Description: 

 

Lebanon continues to face one of the world’s most severe economic and financial crises, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Port of Beirut explosion, and the 2023-2024 conflict. These consecutive shocks have severely weakened labor market prospects, increased unemployment, and expanded poverty. Traditional employment pathways are increasingly constrained due to business closures, limited job creation, and instability.

 

At the same time, digital transformation and remote gig work are reshaping global labor markets. Microwork, small, simple digital tasks such as data tagging, transcription, verification, or AI data labeling, offers accessible, flexible income opportunities for individuals with basic digital literacy. Its low entry barriers make it particularly suitable for poor and vulnerable youth, women, and refugees.

 

The DSE project aims to equip youth and women with market-relevant digital skills and linking them to real income-generating opportunities, the Project supports Lebanon’s recovery from different crises while advancing WBG MENA strategies on human capital, economic inclusion, gender equality, and a resilient, future-ready workforce.

 

Under the DSE project, the Digital Skills for Employment (DSE) builds on global experiences in Economic Inclusion (EI) programs and adapts them to a digital context, replacing traditional asset transfers with tablets or smartphones and pairing skills training with coaching and direct linkage to online income opportunities.





 

  1. Objective and Scope of work: 

 

The Digital Trainers under the Digital Skills for Employment (DSE) Project are responsible for delivering high-quality, inclusive, and market-relevant digital training programs for youth and adults in Lebanon. The trainers will deliver assigned structured training modules covering technical digital skills (data labeling, data collection, call center/customer service, Google tools, and graphic design), soft skills (communication, leadership, time management, critical thinking, self-marketing, and business ethics), digital safety (cybersecurity and responsible online behavior), and financial literacy (online payments, taxation, and income tracking). The Digital Opportunity Trust (DOT Lebanon) has received financing from the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (the World Bank), acting as administrator of the Japan Social Development Fund (JSDF Grant No. TF0D1200) and the Dutch PROSPECTS Fund (MDTF-FD Grant No. TF0D1059), toward the cost of the Digital Skilling for Employment (DSE) Project, and intends to apply part of the proceeds for consulting services.

 

The DSE Project aims to equip vulnerable youth and women across Lebanon with market-relevant digital skills and link them to real income-generating opportunities. Under Component 2: Productive Inclusion in the Digital Economy (Microwork)—specifically Subcomponent 2.2 (JSDF and PROSPECTS Package of Services for Microwork Inclusion)—DOT Lebanon provides digital, technical, and soft skills training paired with coaching, platform profile creation, and direct linkage to online microwork opportunities.

 

2. Objective & Scope of the Assignment

DOT Lebanon is seeking a qualified Individual Consultant to serve as Digital Trainer, reporting directly to the Area Manager. Lebanon continues to face one of the world’s most severe economic and financial crises, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Port of Beirut explosion, and the 2023-2024 conflict. These consecutive shocks have severely weakened labor market prospects, increased unemployment, and expanded poverty. Traditional employment pathways are increasingly constrained due to business closures, limited job creation, and instability.

 

At the same time, digital transformation and remote gig work are reshaping global labor markets. Microwork, small, simple digital tasks such as data tagging, transcription, verification, or AI data labeling, offers accessible, flexible income opportunities for individuals with basic digital literacy. Its low entry barriers make it particularly suitable for poor and vulnerable youth, women, and refugees.

 

The DSE project aims to equip youth and women with market-relevant digital skills and linking them to real income-generating opportunities, the Project supports Lebanon’s recovery from different crises while advancing WBG MENA strategies on human capital, economic inclusion, gender equality, and a resilient, future-ready workforce.

Lebanon continues to face one of the world’s most severe economic and financial crises, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Port of Beirut explosion, and the 2023-2024 conflict. These consecutive shocks have severely weakened labor market prospects, increased unemployment, and expanded poverty. Traditional employment pathways are increasingly constrained due to business closures, limited job creation, and instability.

 

At the same time, digital transformation and remote gig work are reshaping global labor markets. Microwork, small, simple digital tasks such as data tagging, transcription, verification, or AI data labeling, offers accessible, flexible income opportunities for individuals with basic digital literacy. Its low entry barriers make it particularly suitable for poor and vulnerable youth, women, and refugees.

 

The DSE project aims to equip youth and women with market-relevant digital skills and linking them to real income-generating opportunities, the Project supports Lebanon’s recovery from different crises while advancing WBG MENA strategies on human capital, economic inclusion, gender equality, and a resilient, future-ready workforce.

 

Under the DSE project, the Digital Skills for Employment (DSE) builds on global experiences in Economic Inclusion (EI) programs and adapts them to a digital context, replacing traditional asset transfers with tablets or smartphones and pairing skills training with coaching and direct linkage to online income opportunities.

The assignment falls under Component 2: Productive Inclusion in the Digital Economy (Microwork), which prepares vulnerable youth to participate in microwork opportunities through practical skills, mentorship, and access to freelance opportunities. DOT Lebanon is responsible for implementing Component 2.

Under Component 2, Subcomponent 2.1: Supply and Demand Assessment includes the assessment of youth baseline skills and constraints, local, regional, and global microwork demand, potential digital employment sectors, and clients and microwork platforms for partnership and micro-job creation. Subcomponent 2.2: JSDF and PROSPECTS Package of Services for Microwork Inclusion includes digital, technical and soft skills training, coaching and support to complete microtasks, profile creation on microwork platforms, and linkage to microwork opportunities.

 

  1. General Introduction & Grant Description: 

 

Lebanon continues to face one of the world’s most severe economic and financial crises, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Port of Beirut explosion, and the 2023-2024 conflict. These consecutive shocks have severely weakened labor market prospects, increased unemployment, and expanded poverty. Traditional employment pathways are increasingly constrained due to business closures, limited job creation, and instability.

 

At the same time, digital transformation and remote gig work are reshaping global labor markets. Microwork, small, simple digital tasks such as data tagging, transcription, verification, or AI data labeling, offers accessible, flexible income opportunities for individuals with basic digital literacy. Its low entry barriers make it particularly suitable for poor and vulnerable youth, women, and refugees.

 

The DSE project aims to equip youth and women with market-relevant digital skills and linking them to real income-generating opportunities, the Project supports Lebanon’s recovery from different crises while advancing WBG MENA strategies on human capital, economic inclusion, gender equality, and a resilient, future-ready workforce.

 

Under the DSE project, the Digital Skills for Employment (DSE) builds on global experiences in Economic Inclusion (EI) programs and adapts them to a digital context, replacing traditional asset transfers with tablets or smartphones and pairing skills training with coaching and direct linkage to online income opportunities.





 

  1. Objective and Scope of work: 

 

The Digital Trainers under the Digital Skills for Employment (DSE) Project are responsible for delivering high-quality, inclusive, and market-relevant digital training programs for youth and adults in Lebanon. Microwork is a central pathway under DSE, providing participants with an accessible entry point to online income-generating opportunities. The Digital Trainers contribute directly to this pathway by building the practical digital and employability-oriented skills participants need to engage in microwork, freelancing, and other digital employment opportunities.

 

The trainers will deliver assigned structured training modules covering technical digital skills (data labeling, data collection, call center/customer service, Google tools, and graphic design), soft skills (communication, leadership, time management, critical thinking, self-marketing, and business ethics), digital safety (cybersecurity and responsible online behavior), and financial literacy (online payments, taxation, and income tracking). DOT Lebanon will provide the approved curricula, training materials, learning resources, and assessment tools. Trainers are responsible for delivery and are not expected to develop or revise the curriculum or training content. They may adapt facilitation techniques and delivery methodologies to participants’ learning needs, but any substantive modification to the approved content requires prior approval from DOT Lebanon. Trainers will be assigned to modules according to their qualifications and demonstrated expertise; one trainer is not expected to cover the full range of technical, financial literacy, digital safety, and soft-skills topics.

 

The Digital Trainers will also ensure a safe and inclusive learning environment in line with DOT Lebanon safeguarding standards. They will be trained and certified on Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) by the PSEA Focal Point and are required to comply with all safeguarding, child protection, and ethical conduct policies. They will coordinate closely with Area Managers and Field Officers to ensure smooth implementation, participant engagement, and effective monitoring of training activities. The assignment covers 74 training groups in total, to be distributed among 8 Digital Trainers according to the DSE implementation schedule. Each group is expected to include approximately 25 participants. Under JSDF, each cohort receives 36 hours of training (12 sessions of 3 hours); under PROSPECTS, each cohort receives 72 hours of training (24 sessions of 3 hours). Training will be delivered in person across Lebanon. The training schedule will be coordinated between the relevant Area Manager, Trainer, and participants. The actual number of cohorts, sessions, beneficiaries, locations, and monthly assignments allocated to each trainer will be determined by DOT Lebanon based on implementation needs and reflected in the approved assignment schedule.

 

  1. Expected Deliverables and Reporting:

The Digital Trainer shall deliver assigned training sessions according to the agreed schedule and DOT Lebanon-approved curricula and materials; maintain attendance records; administer and document approved pre- and post-assessments, assignments, and practical exercises, as applicable; submit a timesheet monthly for payment purposes; and submit a simple cohort completion report upon completion of each assigned cohort.

The cohort completion report shall be submitted to the relevant Area Manager using a simple format provided or approved by DOT Lebanon and shall include, at a minimum, sessions delivered, attendance, assessment completion and results where applicable, key observations or challenges, and any required follow-up. Attendance records and session-level documentation shall be maintained and submitted in accordance with DOT Lebanon procedures.

The Digital Opportunity Trust (DOT Lebanon) (the Recipient) will implement the Digital Skilling for Employment (DSE) Project, as set out in the Grant Agreement (the Agreement). The International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (the Bank), acting as the administrator of the JSDF Fund and the Dutch PROSPECTS Fund, has agreed to provide financing for the Project, as set out in the Agreement.

The assignment falls under Component 2: Productive Inclusion in the Digital Economy (Microwork), which prepares vulnerable youth to participate in microwork opportunities through practical skills, mentorship, and access to freelance opportunities. DOT Lebanon is responsible for implementing Component 2.

Under Component 2, Subcomponent 2.1: Supply and Demand Assessment includes the assessment of youth baseline skills and constraints, local, regional, and global microwork demand, potential digital employment sectors, and clients and microwork platforms for partnership and micro-job creation. Subcomponent 2.2: JSDF and PROSPECTS Package of Services for Microwork Inclusion includes digital, technical and soft skills training, coaching and support to complete microtasks, profile creation on microwork platforms, and linkage to microwork opportunities.

 

  1. General Introduction & Grant Description: 

 

Lebanon continues to face one of the world’s most severe economic and financial crises, compounded by the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic, the Port of Beirut explosion, and the 2023-2024 conflict. These consecutive shocks have severely weakened labor market prospects, increased unemployment, and expanded poverty. Traditional employment pathways are increasingly constrained due to business closures, limited job creation, and instability.

 

At the same time, digital transformation and remote gig work are reshaping global labor markets. Microwork, small, simple digital tasks such as data tagging, transcription, verification, or AI data labeling, offers accessible, flexible income opportunities for individuals with basic digital literacy. Its low entry barriers make it particularly suitable for poor and vulnerable youth, women, and refugees.

 

The DSE project aims to equip youth and women with market-relevant digital skills and linking them to real income-generating opportunities, the Project supports Lebanon’s recovery from different crises while advancing WBG MENA strategies on human capital, economic inclusion, gender equality, and a resilient, future-ready workforce.

 

Under the DSE project, the Digital Skills for Employment (DSE) builds on global experiences in Economic Inclusion (EI) programs and adapts them to a digital context, replacing traditional asset transfers with tablets or smartphones and pairing skills training with coaching and direct linkage to online income opportunities.





 

  1. Objective and Scope of work: 

 

The Digital Trainers under the Digital Skills for Employment (DSE) Project are responsible for delivering high-quality, inclusive, and market-relevant digital training programs for youth and adults in Lebanon. Microwork is a central pathway under DSE, providing participants with an accessible entry point to online income-generating opportunities. The Digital Trainers contribute directly to this pathway by building the practical digital and employability-oriented skills participants need to engage in microwork, freelancing, and other digital employment opportunities.

 

The trainers will deliver assigned structured training modules covering technical digital skills (data labeling, data collection, call center/customer service, Google tools, and graphic design), soft skills (communication, leadership, time management, critical thinking, self-marketing, and business ethics), digital safety (cybersecurity and responsible online behavior), and financial literacy (online payments, taxation, and income tracking). DOT Lebanon will provide the approved curricula, training materials, learning resources, and assessment tools. Trainers are responsible for delivery and are not expected to develop or revise the curriculum or training content. They may adapt facilitation techniques and delivery methodologies to participants’ learning needs, but any substantive modification to the approved content requires prior approval from DOT Lebanon. Trainers will be assigned to modules according to their qualifications and demonstrated expertise; one trainer is not expected to cover the full range of technical, financial literacy, digital safety, and soft-skills topics.

 

The Digital Trainers will also ensure a safe and inclusive learning environment in line with DOT Lebanon safeguarding standards. They will be trained and certified on Protection from Sexual Exploitation and Abuse (PSEA) by the PSEA Focal Point and are required to comply with all safeguarding, child protection, and ethical conduct policies. They will coordinate closely with Area Managers and Field Officers to ensure smooth implementation, participant engagement, and effective monitoring of training activities. The assignment covers 74 training groups in total, to be distributed among 8 Digital Trainers according to the DSE implementation schedule. Each group is expected to include approximately 25 participants. Under JSDF, each cohort receives 36 hours of training (12 sessions of 3 hours); under PROSPECTS, each cohort receives 72 hours of training (24 sessions of 3 hours). Training will be delivered in person across Lebanon. The training schedule will be coordinated between the relevant Area Manager, Trainer, and participants. The actual number of cohorts, sessions, beneficiaries, locations, and monthly assignments allocated to each trainer will be determined by DOT Lebanon based on implementation needs and reflected in the approved assignment schedule.

 

  1. Expected Deliverables and Reporting:

The Digital Trainer shall deliver assigned training sessions according to the agreed schedule and DOT Lebanon-approved curricula and materials; maintain attendance records; administer and document approved pre- and post-assessments, assignments, and practical exercises, as applicable; submit a timesheet monthly for payment purposes; and submit a simple cohort completion report upon completion of each assigned cohort.

The cohort completion report shall be submitted to the relevant Area Manager using a simple format provided or approved by DOT Lebanon and shall include, at a minimum, sessions delivered, attendance, assessment completion and results where applicable, key observations or challenges, and any required follow-up. Attendance records and session-level documentation shall be maintained and submitted in accordance with DOT Lebanon procedures.

REQUEST FOR EXPRESSIONS OF INTEREST

(CONSULTING SERVICES – FIRMS SELECTION)

FEDERAL DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF ETHIOPIA

LOWLANDS LIVELIHOOD RESILIENCE PROJECT – PHASE II (LLRP-II)

Credit No.: 7519-ET

Assignment Title: Consultancy Services for Planning, Feasibility Study, Environmental and Social Impact Assessment, Detailed Engineering Design and Preparation of Procurement Documents for Climate-Resilient Rural Water Supply and Sanitation Systems Based on New Small/Micro Dams (Haffir Dams) in Aware, Filtu, Dolo-bay, Garbo, Dig and Hararey Woredas, Somali Regional State

Reference No.: ET-SOM- RPCU-570305-CS-QCBS

The Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia has received financing from the International Development Association (IDA) of the World Bank and the International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) toward the cost of the Lowlands Livelihood Resilience Project – Phase II (LLRP-II), and intends to apply part of the proceeds for consulting services.

The consulting services (“the Services”) include planning, feasibility study, environmental and social impact assessment, detailed engineering design and preparation of procurement documents for six (6) climate-resilient rural piped water supply and sanitation schemes based on new small/micro dams (haffir dams), serving pastoral and agro-pastoral communities in Somali Regional State, namely: (1) Aware 01 kebele, Aware Woreda, Jarar Zone; (2) Anobeden kebele, Filtu Woreda, Liban Zone; (3) Darso kebele, Dolo-bay Woreda, Afdher Zone ; (4) Goldhabiley kebele, Garbo Woreda, Nogob Zone; (5) Dig-01 kebele, Dig Woreda, Jarar Zone; and (6) Hararey 01 kebele, Hararey Woreda, Nogob Zone. Each scheme is expected to comprise a new small/micro dam (an excavated haffir with perimeter embankment or a small embankment dam) with its inlet and abstraction works and, as required, water treatment, solar-powered pumping, transmission, storage, distribution, public water points, livestock watering facilities, and public and institutional sanitation facilities. Groundwater may be considered as an alternative or supplementary source where justified. Detailed designs and procurement documents will be prepared only for the schemes approved by the Client following the feasibility study.

The Services comprise: review of existing information and preparation of an Inception Report, including a site-specific dam investigation and testing programme and preliminary dam hazard screening; reconnaissance survey and baseline assessment; stakeholder consultation, conducted in Somali, with communities, customary institutions, women, youth, vulnerable groups and seasonal water users; socioeconomic, gender and social inclusion, existing service level and institutional capacity assessments; water demand assessment for domestic, livestock and institutional uses, including dry-season peaks; surface water investigation (catchment hydrology, flood frequency, sediment and water balance) and a site-specific reservoir storage–yield and reliability analysis for each dam; verification of groundwater information where groundwater is considered; feasibility study, including analysis of alternatives, economic and financial analysis, climate risk and resilience assessment, and a site-by-site feasibility decision; topographic, geotechnical and dam site investigations (foundations, abutments, reservoir basin, permeability, borrow areas and laboratory testing); environmental and social screening and impact assessment and preparation of the applicable ESF instruments (ESIA/ESMP, SEP, LMP, resettlement instruments where required, and GBV/SEA/SH and community health and safety measures) in accordance with the World Bank Environmental and Social Framework (ESF) and IFAD requirements; climate-resilient detailed engineering design of the dams and appurtenant structures (spillways, outlet works, seepage control and sediment management), intakes, treatment where required, solar pumping, transmission, storage, distribution, water points, livestock watering and sanitation facilities; dam safety classification and measures in accordance with World Bank ESS4; operation and maintenance strategies and manuals, including a spare parts market assessment; construction scheduling; capacity building of Client staff; and preparation of procurement documents based on the World Bank Standard Procurement Documents (technical specifications, drawings, bills of quantities and confidential Engineer’s cost estimates) for each approved scheme.

The implementation period is three (3) calendar months from the date of commencement, and the assignment is expected to start in December 2026.

The detailed Terms of Reference (TOR) for the assignment can be obtained at the address given below.

Somali Regional State, Office of the President, Lowlands Livelihood Resilience Project (LLRP-II) Regional Project Coordination Unit now invites eligible consulting firms (“Consultants”) to indicate their interest in providing the Services. Interested Consultants should provide information demonstrating that they have the required qualifications and relevant experience to perform the Services. The shortlisting criteria are:

(a)  Core business and years in business: the firm’s core business shall be in water supply and sanitation and/or water resources engineering consultancy services (studies and design). Provide the company profile, certificate of registration, and number of years in business.

(b)  General experience: experience in consultancy services (studies, design and/or construction supervision) for water supply, sanitation, dams or other water resources infrastructure during the last ten (10) years.

(c)  Specific experience: experience in assignments of similar nature and complexity, i.e. feasibility studies, environmental and social impact assessment and detailed engineering design of rural or small-town water supply and sanitation systems, and the planning and design of small dams, haffirs or other surface water storage structures (including hydrological and reservoir storage–yield analysis, geotechnical and dam site investigations, spillway design and dam safety), together with preparation of bidding documents, preferably in arid, semi-arid or pastoral/agro-pastoral lowland areas of Ethiopia and under projects financed by the World Bank or other international development partners, including application of the World Bank ESF (and, where relevant, ESS4 dam safety requirements). For each assignment, indicate the client, location, population served and/or dam size (height and storage), contract value, duration, scope of services and the firm’s role, supported by contract or completion certificates.

(d) Technical and managerial capability of the firm: organizational structure, survey equipment (e.g. GNSS/GPS and total stations), access to accredited soil/geotechnical and water quality laboratories, hydrological, hydraulic network (e.g. WaterCAD/EPANET), structural, seepage/slope stability and GIS software, quality assurance systems, and capacity to mobilize multidisciplinary field teams, including parallel teams and Somali-speaking staff, to remote and geographically dispersed areas of Somali Region, and to manage field health, safety and security risks.

Key Experts will not be evaluated at the shortlisting stage.

The attention of interested Consultants is drawn to Section III, paragraphs 3.14, 3.16, and 3.17 of the World Bank’s “Procurement Regulations for IPF Borrowers” September 2023 (“Procurement Regulations”), setting forth the World Bank’s policy on conflict of interest.

Consultants may associate with other firms to enhance their qualifications, but should indicate clearly whether the association is in the form of a joint venture and/or a sub-consultancy. In the case of a joint venture, all the partners in the joint venture shall be jointly and severally liable for the entire contract, if selected.

A Consultant will be selected in accordance with the Quality- and Cost-Based Selection (QCBS) method set out in the Procurement Regulations.

The Government of Vanuatu (Gov) has received financing from the World Bank toward the cost of the Pacific Islands Regional Oceanscape Program (PROP) and intends to apply part of the proceeds for consulting services.

The consulting services (“the Services”) is to support the project support team to meet the commitments of the Vanuatu PROP Environmental and Social Commitment Plan and comply with the World Bank Environmental and Social Framework (ESF) and Vauatu laws and regulations.         

The Ministry of Fisheries, Ocean and Maritime Affairs (MFOMA) now invite eligible individuals (“Consultants”) to indicate their interest in providing the Services. Interested Consultants should provide information demonstrating that they have the required qualifications and relevant experience to perform the Services (attach curriculum vitae with description of experience in similar assignments, similar conditions, etc.). Experience:

  • At least 10 years experience related to the management of Environmental and Social risks associated with large scale infrastructure, including implementing ecological surveys and undertaking ecological impact assessment in a coastal or marine context.
  • Managed or held a senior position in at least five environmental and social impact assessment projects for infrastructure projects.
  • Demonstrated experience as a peer reviewer, project director, technical director or similar in their field of expertise.
  • Demonstrated experience working with World Bank Environmental and Social Standards or similar.  Experience applying ESS6, IFC Performance Standard 6 or similar is desirable.

  • Fluency in written and spoken English.
  • High quality writing and presentation skills.
  • Familiarity with ni-Vanuatu culture and Bislama is an advantage.

  • Ability to deliver effective and engaging training sessions to a variety of participants.

LAND SPECIALIST

 

Vanuatu

 

Pacific Islands Regional Oceanscape Program - First Phase Project

Preparation Advance No. V555-VU

Reference: VU-MFOMA-570882-CS-INDV

 

The Government of Vanuatu (Gov) has received financing from the World Bank toward the cost of the Pacific Islands Regional Oceanscape Program (PROP) and intends to apply part of the proceeds for consulting services.

The consulting services (“the Services”) include clarifying land tenure status for all Project sites; advise on and support the appropriate land access and permitting processes, including foreshore development requirements; ensuring compliance with including Environmental and Social Standards ESS5 (Land Acquisition, Restrictions on Land Use and Involuntary Resettlement) and ESS7 (Indigenous Peoples / Historically Underserved Traditional Local Communities commitments in the Environmental and Social Commitment Plan; and supporting Ministry of Fisheries, Ocean and Maritime Affairs engaging with relevant government agencies and, where required, customary landowners and traditional authorities. The assignment is parttime and intermittent with an estimated level of effort of 110 days.

The Ministry of Fisheries, Ocean and Maritime Affairs now invite eligible individuals (“Consultants”) to indicate their interest in providing the Services. Interested Consultants should provide information demonstrating that they have the required qualifications and relevant experience to perform the Services (attach curriculum vitae with description of experience in similar assignments, similar conditions, etc.). Firms’ staff may express interest through the employing firm for the assignment and, under such situation, only the experience and qualifications of individuals shall be considered in the selection process. The criteria for selecting the Consultant are:

Required Qualifications and Experience

A. Mandatory Qualifications and Experience

The Land Specialist must have:

  • Advanced degree in land administration, law, planning, natural resource management or a related field.
  • At least 8–10 years of demonstrated experience in land tenure, land access, land administration or land related legal and regulatory processes, preferably in Vanuatu or comparable Pacific Island contexts Strong understanding of customary land and marine tenure systems.
  • Strong analytical and advisory skills, with the ability to produce clear, practical guidance.
  • Demonstrated experience working with customary land tenure systems, including engagement with customary landowners, traditional authorities and community governance structures is desirable.

B. Desirable Qualifications and Experience

The following will be considered an advantage:

  • Familiarity with World Bank ESS5 and ESS7, including FPIC requirements.
  • Experience in Vanuatu or comparable Pacific Island contexts, particularly in relation to land tenure, land access and land administration.
  • Experience addressing foreshore, seabed or marine tenure issues, including permitting or access processes affecting coastal or marine areas is desirable.
  • Demonstrated knowledge of Vanuatu land, foreshore and related permitting frameworks, including land allocation, leasing, municipal/state land, and foreshore development processes is desirable
  • Experience coordinating with government agencies responsible for land, planning, foreshore or natural resource management is desirable.
  • Experience working with development partners, particularly on projects involving World Bank environmental and social requirements

The attention of interested Consultants (including firms) is drawn to paragraph 3.14, 3.16 and 3.17 of the World Bank’s Procurement Regulations for IPF Borrowers Seventh Edition September 2025 as per financing agreement (“the Regulations”), setting forth the World Bank’s policy on conflict of interest.

Instructions to Consultants

A.  General Provisions

1. Definitions

  1. “Affiliate(s)” means an individual or an entity that directly or indirectly controls, is controlled by, or is under common control with the Consultant.
  2. “Applicable Law” means the laws and any other instruments having the force of law in the Client’s country, or in such other country as may be specified in the Data Sheet, as they may be issued and in force from time to time.

  6.  “Client’s Personnel” is as defined in Clause GCC 1.1 (e).

  9. “Data Sheet” means an integral part of the Instructions to Consultants (ITC) Section 2 that is used to reflect specific country and assignment conditions to supplement, but not to over-write, the provisions of the ITC.
  10. “Day” means a calendar day, unless otherwise specified as “Business Day”. A Business Day is any day that is an official working day of the Borrower. It excludes the Borrower’s official public holidays.
  11. “Experts” means, collectively, Key Experts, Non-Key Experts, or any other personnel of the Consultant, Sub-consultant or Joint Venture member(s).
  12. “Government” means the government of the Client’s country.
  13. “in writing” means communicated in written form (e.g. by mail, e-mail, fax, including, if specified in the Data Sheet, distributed or received through the electronic-procurement system used by the Client) with proof of receipt.
  14. “Joint Venture (JV)” means an association with or without a legal personality distinct from that of its members, of more than one Consultant where one member has the authority to conduct all business for and on behalf of any and all the members of the JV, and where the members of the JV are jointly and severally liable to the Client for the performance of the Contract.
  15. “Key Expert(s)” means an individual professional whose skills, qualifications, knowledge and experience are critical to the performance of the Services under the Contract and whose CV is taken into account in the technical evaluation of the Consultant’s proposal.
  16. “ITC” (this Section 2 of the RFP) means the Instructions to Consultants that provides the Consultants with all information needed to prepare their Proposals.
  17. “Non-Key Expert(s)” means an individual professional provided by the Consultant or its Sub-consultant and who is assigned to perform the Services or any part thereof under the Contract and whose CVs are not evaluated individually.
  18. “Proposal” means the Technical Proposal and the Financial Proposal of the Consultant.
  19. “RFP” means the Request for Proposals to be prepared by the Client for the selection of Consultants, based on the SPD - RFP.
  20. “Services” means the work to be performed by the Consultant pursuant to the Contract.
  21. “SPD - RFP” means the Standard Procurement Document - Request for Proposals, which must be used by the Client as the basis for the preparation of the RFP.
  22. “Sub-consultant” means an entity to whom the Consultant intends to subcontract any part of the Services while the Consultant remains responsible to the Client during the whole performance of the Contract.
  23. “Terms of Reference (TORs)” (this Section 7 of the RFP) means the Terms of Reference that explains the objectives, scope of work, activities, and tasks to be performed, respective responsibilities of the Client and the Consultant, and expected results and deliverables of the assignment.

2. Introduction

    1. The Client named in the Data Sheet intends to select a Consultant from those listed in the Request for Proposals (RFP), in accordance with the method of selection specified in the Data Sheet.
    2. The Consultants are invited to submit a Technical Proposal and a Financial Proposal, or a Technical Proposal only, as specified in the Data Sheet, for consulting services required for the assignment named in the Data Sheet. The Proposal will be the basis for negotiating and ultimately signing the Contract with the selected Consultant.
    3. The Consultants should familiarize themselves with the local conditions and take them into account in preparing their Proposals, including attending a pre-proposal conference if one is specified in the Data Sheet. Attending any such pre-proposal conference is optional and is at the Consultants’ expense.
    4. The Client will timely provide, at no cost to the Consultants, the inputs, relevant project data, and reports required for the preparation of the Consultant’s Proposal as specified in the Data Sheet.

3. Conflict of Interest

    1. The Consultant is required to provide professional, objective, and impartial advice, at all times holding the Client’s interests paramount, strictly avoiding conflicts with other assignments or its own corporate interests, and acting without any consideration for future work.
    2. The Consultant has an obligation to disclose to the Client any situation of actual or potential conflict that impacts its capacity to serve the best interest of its Client. Failure to disclose such situations may lead to the disqualification of the Consultant or the termination of its Contract and/or sanctions by the Bank.
      1. Without limitation on the generality of the foregoing, the Consultant shall not be hired under the circumstances set forth below:

a.  Conflicting Activities

(i)      Conflict between consulting activities and procurement of goods, works or non-consulting services: a firm that has been engaged by the Client to provide goods, works, or non-consulting services for a project, or any of its Affiliates, shall be disqualified from providing consulting services resulting from or directly related to those goods, works, or non-consulting services. Conversely, a firm hired to provide consulting services for the preparation or implementation of a project, or any of its Affiliates, shall be disqualified from subsequently providing goods or works or non-consulting services resulting from or directly related to the consulting services for such preparation or implementation.

b.  Conflicting Assignments

(ii)     Conflict among consulting assignments: a Consultant (including its Experts and Sub-consultants) or any of its Affiliates shall not be hired for any assignment that, by its nature, may be in conflict with another assignment of the Consultant for the same or for another Client.

c. Conflicting Relationships

(iii)    Relationship with the Client’s staff: a Consultant (including its Experts and Sub-consultants) that has a close business or family relationship with a professional staff  of the Borrower (or of the Client, or of implementing agency, or of a recipient of a part of the Bank’s financing) who are directly or indirectly involved in any part of (i) the preparation of the Terms of Reference for the assignment, (ii) the selection process for the Contract, or (iii) the supervision of the Contract, may not be awarded a Contract, unless the conflict stemming from this relationship has been resolved in a manner acceptable to the Bank throughout the selection process and the execution of the Contract.

4. Unfair Competitive Advantage

    1. Fairness and transparency in the selection process require that the Consultants or their Affiliates competing for a specific assignment do not derive a competitive advantage from having provided consulting services related to the assignment in question. To that end, the Client shall indicate in the Data Sheet and make available to all Consultants together with this RFP all information that would in that respect give such Consultant any unfair competitive advantage over competing Consultants. 

5. Fraud and Corruption

    1. The Bank requires compliance with the Bank’s Anti-Corruption Guidelines and its prevailing sanctions policies and procedures as set forth in the WBG’s Sanctions Framework, as set forth in Section 6.
    2. In further pursuance of this policy, Consultants shall permit and shall cause their agents (where declared or not), subcontractors, subconsultants, service providers, suppliers, and personnel, to permit the Bank to inspect all accounts, records and other documents relating to any shortlisting process, Proposal submission, and contract performance (in the case of award), and to have them audited by auditors appointed by the Bank.

6. Eligibility

    1. The Bank permits consultants (individuals and firms, including Joint Ventures and their individual members) from all countries to offer consulting services for Bank-financed projects.
    2. Furthermore, it is the Consultant’s responsibility to ensure that its Experts, joint venture members, Sub-consultants, agents (declared or not), sub-contractors, service providers, suppliers and/or their employees meet the eligibility requirements as established by the Bank in the applicable Procurement Regulations.
    3. As an exception to the foregoing ITC 6.1 and ITC 6.2 above:

a. Sanctions

      1. A Consultant that has been sanctioned by the Bank, pursuant to the Bank’s Anti-Corruption Guidelines and in accordance with its prevailing sanctions policies and procedures as set forth in the WBG’s Sanctions Framework as described in Section VI, Fraud and Corruption, paragraph 2.2 d., shall be ineligible to be shortlisted for, submit proposals for, or be awarded a Bank-financed contract or benefit from a Bank-financed contract, financially or otherwise, during such period of time as the Bank shall have determined. The list of debarred firms and individuals is available at the electronic address specified in the Data Sheet.

b. Prohibitions

      1. Firms and individuals of a country or goods manufactured in a country may be ineligible if so indicated in Section 5 (Eligible Countries) and:

(a)    as a matter of law or official regulations, the Borrower’s country prohibits commercial relations with that country, provided that the Bank is satisfied that such exclusion does not preclude effective competition for the provision of Services required; or

(b)   by an act of compliance with a decision of the United Nations Security Council taken under Chapter VII of the Charter of the United Nations, the Borrower’s Country prohibits any import of goods from that country or any payments to any country, person, or entity in that country.

c. Restrictions for State-Owned Enterprises

      1. State-owned enterprises or institutions in the Borrower’s country may be eligible to compete and be awarded a contract only if they can establish, in a manner acceptable to the Bank, that they: (i) are legally and financially autonomous, (ii) operate under commercial law, and (iii) are not under supervision of the Client. 

d. Restrictions for Public Employees

      1. Government officials and civil servants of the Borrower’s country are not eligible to be included as Experts, individuals, or members of a team of Experts in the Consultant’s Proposal unless:

(i) the services of the government official or civil servant are of a unique and exceptional nature, or their participation is critical to project implementation; and

(ii) their hiring would not create a conflict of interest, including any conflict with employment or other laws, regulations, or policies of the Borrower.

B.  Preparation of Proposals

7. General Considerations

    1. In preparing the Proposal, the Consultant is expected to examine the RFP in detail. Material deficiencies in providing the information requested in the RFP may result in rejection of the Proposal.

8. Cost of Preparation of Proposal

    1. The Consultant shall bear all costs associated with the preparation and submission of its Proposal, and the Client shall not be responsible or liable for those costs, regardless of the conduct or outcome of the selection process. P = 20%

Appendix A. Financial Negotiations - Breakdown of Remuneration Rates

  1. Review of Remuneration Rates
    1. The remuneration rates are made up of salary or a base fee, social costs, overheads, profit, and any premium or allowance that may be paid for assignments away from headquarters or a home office.  An attached Sample Form can be used to provide a breakdown of rates.
    2. If the RFP requests submission of a technical proposal only, the Sample Form is used by the selected Consultant to prepare for the negotiations of the Contract. If the RFP requests submission of the financial proposal, the Sample Form shall be completed and attached to the Financial Form-3.  Agreed (at the negotiations) breakdown sheets shall form part of the negotiated Contract and included in its Appendix D or C.
    3. At the negotiations the firm shall be prepared to disclose its audited financial statements for the last three years, to substantiate its rates, and accept that its proposed rates and other financial matters are subject to scrutiny.  The Client is charged with the custody of government funds and is expected to exercise prudence in the expenditure of these funds. 
    4. Rate details are discussed below:
  1. Salary is the gross regular cash salary or fee paid to the individual in the firm’s home office.  It shall not contain any premium for work away from headquarters or bonus (except where these are included by law or government regulations).
  2. Bonuses are normally paid out of profits.  To avoid double counting, any bonuses shall not normally be included in the “Salary” and should be shown separately.  Where the Consultant’s accounting system is such that the percentages of social costs and overheads are based on total revenue, including bonuses, those percentages shall be adjusted downward accordingly.  Where national policy requires that 13 months’ pay be given for 12 months’ work, the profit element need not be adjusted downward.  Any discussions on bonuses shall be supported by audited documentation, which shall be treated as confidential.
  3. Social Charges are the costs of non-monetary benefits and may include, inter alia, social security (including pension, medical, and life insurance costs) and the cost of a paid sick and/or annual leave.  In this regard, a paid leave during public holidays or an annual leave taken during an assignment if no Expert’s replacement has been provided is not considered social charges.

  1. Overheads are the Consultant’s business costs that are not directly related to the execution of the assignment and shall not be reimbursed as separate items under the Contract. Typical items are home office costs (non-billable time, time of senior Consultant’s staff monitoring the project, rent of headquarters’ office, support staff, research, staff training, marketing, etc.), the cost of Consultant’s personnel not currently employed on revenue-earning projects, taxes on business activities, and business promotion costs.   2. Profit is normally based on the sum of the Salary, Social costs, and Overheads.  If any bonuses paid on a regular basis are listed, a corresponding reduction shall be made in the profit amount. Profit shall not be allowed on travel or any other reimbursable expenses.
  3. Away from Home Office Allowance or Premium or Subsistence Allowances. Some Consultants pay allowances to Experts working away from headquarters or outside of the home office.  Such allowances are calculated as a percentage of salary (or a fee) and shall not draw overheads or profit.  Sometimes, by law, such allowances may draw social costs.  In this case, the amount of this social cost shall still be shown under social costs, with the net allowance shown separately.

Section 7.  Terms of Reference

  1. Background:

The West Bengal Health System Reform Program (WBHSRP) Operation is a health systems reforms program of the Department of Health and Family Welfare (DoH&FW), Govt. of West Bengal (GoWB). The WBHSRP is implemented during 2025-2031, with US$286 million loan from the World Bank and would use a Program for Results (PforR) lending instrument that focuses on result-based outcomes, with a Technical Assistance [TA]/IPF component to ensure focus on results-based outcomes for achieving the Program Development Objectives (PDO). This assignment is under the Technical Assistance component of the WBHSRP.

 

The Program Development Objective (PDO) of the WBHSRP is “to improve utilization of health services, enhance quality of care and reduce inequities in maternal and adolescent health in West Bengal”. The program activities are organized around the four Result Areas (RAs) which contribute to the PDO. The activities of the WBHSRP under the four result areas (RAs) principally are such that they either expedite, augment or enhance the existing government program.

  1. Results Area 1: Strengthened integrated care model for CPHC services
  2. Results Area 2: Reduced health inequalities in maternal and adolescent health
  3. Results Area 3: Enhanced Governance, Accountability and Resilience
  4. Results Area 4: Alignment of behaviors between people and Providers

 

RA-1: Strengthened integrated care model for CPHC services: The key focus of this RA is to strengthen the policies and service delivery framework to address the NCD related risk factors, improve input and process quality of the primary healthcare system, strengthen the continuum of care, and streamline protocols for frontline workers and service providers for the provision of quality personalized care. Global evidence suggests that addressing risk factors early on leads to a reduction in the disease burden for NCD and facilitating processes and protocols for the providers has a positive impact on care-seeking among NCD patients, ultimately leads to control of NCD conditions.[6]  While the focus of the RA is on hypertension and diabetes, strengthened systems are expected to improve access and quality of services for other NCDs.

 

RA#2: Reduced health inequalities in maternal and adolescent health: RA#2 will strengthen the delivery of health services to address the challenges of adolescent girls and boys. While several interventions targeting adolescents are operational in the state, gaps remain in their coverage and quality, coordination, and monitoring mechanisms. Addressing the GBV also requires streamlining key interventions within the health system. Thus, the design of RA#2 seeks to (a) strengthen convergence among DoHFW, School Education Department and Women and Child Development Department and track key indicators and progress at the state, district and sub-district levels; (b) expand coverage and quality of RKSK program; and (c) develop and roll out survivor-centric GBV services

 

RA #3 – Enhanced Governance, Accountability and Resilience: This RA focuses on critical QoC interventions, which are recognized through global evidence to be the ‘best buys’ on governance, accountability and resilience.[7] These include developing a facility- and administrative-level performance measurement framework (PMF) to track progress of health system performance and public reporting and facility accreditation for comprehensive emergency obstetric and newborn care (CEmONC) centers.[8] Additionally, this result would focus on strengthening public financial management (PFM) and procurement-related challenges, which are critical to improve governance. Finally, the RA would also focus on extreme weather events and health-related interventions and strengthening the climate resilience of the health system.

 

RA#4: Alignment of behaviors between people and Providers: RA#4 would strengthen the system to address people and provider behaviors. It will support development and implementation of social and behavior change communication (SBCC) strategies to improve maternal and adolescent health and GBV-related outcomes, especially in priority districts lagging the state averages. The interventions are expected to empower communities with knowledge and awareness about health risks and available services. RA#4 will also support activities to bridge providers’ know-do gap for better clinical effectiveness. These interventions are well defined under several global frameworks[9], and proven to improve quality of services and increase demand.

 

A key element under Results Area 1 is the control and prevention of NCDs, notably hypertension and diabetes, which account for a growing burden of morbidity and mortality in the state. The Global status report on Non-Communicable Diseases by World Health Organization (WHO) has estimated that every year, nearly 28 million people lose their lives to NCDs. In India, NCDs account for 60% of the total deaths. The burden of NCDs and associated risk factors is evident worldwide. This is especially true among those living in poverty. NCDs are increasingly affecting developing countries at a faster rate than in developed nations. NCDs are lifestyle diseases, as the behavioural risk factors like smoking, alcohol consumption, inadequate fruit and vegetables intake and physical inactivity pose an individual at increased risk of developing NCD. Although many lifestyle factors are considered to be modifiable, all individuals, across all strata of society should have sufficient and equal access and support to make healthy lifestyle choices. The WHO global status report on non-communicable diseases 2010 ranked the monitoring and surveillance of risk factors as a top priority to tackle growing NCD epidemics in low resource settings.  India, as part of Integrated Disease Surveillance Project, conducted a NCD risk factor surveillance using WHO STEPS questionnaire in the year 2007 to provide data on risk factors, which in turn was expecting to help the state health administrators to plan strategies for the control of non-communicable diseases by modifying the risk factors. Though it was planned to include all Indian states in a phased manner, the project ended with the first phase which included seven states namely Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Mizoram, Tamil Nadu and Uttarakhand.

 

West Bengal has not conducted this survey in the past and having combated the major communicable diseases in West Bengal, it is high time that the resources are invested on fighting non- communicable diseases.  To address this, the Department of Health & Family Welfare (DoHFW), Government of West Bengal (GoWB) plans to undertake a state-wide STEPwise approach to NCD risk factor surveillance (STEPS)[10] aligned with the WHO’s standardized approach for surveillance of NCD risk factors. This will provide critical baseline data to inform policy, measure program performance, and strengthen the quality of primary care service delivery under WBHSRP.

 

  1. Objective of the Assignment

The overall objective of the assignment is to conduct a comprehensive NCD risk factor survey in West Bengal based on the WHO STEPS methodology targeting adult population (18-69 years), so as to generate population level estimates on key NCD risk factors (behaviorial, physical and biochemical) disaggregated by age, gender and geography, in order to ultimately formulate a baseline for the Program to support design of preventive, diagnostic, and treatment strategies.

 

Specific tasks under this objective include but may not be limited to the following :

  1. Assess the prevalence of key NCD behavioural risk factors (tobacco use, alcohol consumption, unhealthy dietary habits, physical inactivity and oral health)
  2. Assess the prevalence of key NCD biological risk factors (high blood pressure, high blood sugar, obesity, high total cholesterol, high LDL, HDL level and thyroid profile)
  3. Assess the knowledge and practice on selected tobacco control policies, alcohol consumption, physical inactivity, unhealthy diet, etc.
  4. Assess the health seeking behaviour related to NCDs.

Annexure I: West Bengal Statewide WHO STEPS Survey

 

Research Proposal and Field Implementation Protocol

 

Assessment of behavioral, physical and biochemical risk factors for noncommunicable diseases among adults aged 18–69 years in West Bengal, India

 

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) are a major and preventable cause of premature mortality, disability and household expenditure. West Bengal requires current, comparable and district-sensitive information on tobacco use, alcohol consumption, diet, physical inactivity, obesity, raised blood pressure, diabetes and dyslipidaemia. This protocol proposes a state-wide, population-representative, cross-sectional survey using the WHO STEP wise approach: Step 1 interview, Step 2 physical measurements and Step 3 biochemical measurements. The target population is adults aged 18–69 years who have lived at the selected address for at least 12 months.

 

The proposed minimum sample is 7,680 completed participants, distributed by population proportion across the 28 administrative survey domains used in the source document, with rural and urban representation. One adult will be selected per household by a documented Kish procedure. The survey will use electronic capture, step-specific sampling weights, complex-survey analysis, laboratory quality assurance, individual feedback and an active referral pathway. The proposal retains the source document’s core design while strengthening the sampling plan, case definitions, safety procedures, governance, data management, indicators and reporting framework.

 

KEY DESIGN PARAMETERS

• Design: Statewide cross-sectional household survey.

• Framework: WHO STEP wise approach, STEPS instrument v3.2, with approved India/West Bengal adaptations.

• Population: Adults 18–69 years, usual residents for ≥12 months.

• Geography: All selected rural and urban primary sampling units in West Bengal.

• Sample: 7,680 completed Step 1 participants; target Step 2 and Step 3 completion will be maximised and reported separately.

• Steps: Step 1 behavioural and health-history interview; Step 2 anthropometry and blood pressure; Step 3 fasting venous blood testing.

• Main outputs: Weighted prevalence, means, 95% confidence intervals, treatment and control cascades, combined-risk-factor burden, rural–urban and sex/age inequalities, district profiles and policy recommendations.

 

1. BACKGROUND AND RATIONALE

NCD prevention requires surveillance of exposure, early disease, treatment and control. The source West Bengal protocol identifies tobacco, alcohol, unhealthy diet, physical inactivity, obesity, blood pressure, glucose, lipids, thyroid testing and health-seeking behavior as priority domains. It also documents the need for a contemporary statewide survey after the limited earlier national surveillance effort.

 

2. OBJECTIVES

2.1 General objective

To estimate the prevalence and distribution of behavioural, physical and biochemical NCD risk factors, and the diagnosis, treatment and control of selected NCD conditions, among adults aged 18–69 years in West Bengal.

 

2.2 Specific objectives

1. Estimate current and daily tobacco use, smokeless tobacco use and second-hand smoke exposure.

2. Estimate alcohol use, heavy episodic drinking and alcohol-related risk indicators.

3. Estimate inadequate fruit and vegetable consumption, salt-related behaviors and dietary risk indicators.

4. Estimate physical activity level, insufficient physical activity and sedentary behavior.

5. Estimate mean BMI, overweight, obesity, central obesity and waist-to-hip ratio.

6. Estimate mean blood pressure and prevalence of raised blood pressure.

7. Estimate fasting glucose, diabetes, impaired fasting glucose, total cholesterol, HDL cholesterol and triglycerides, subject to laboratory feasibility.

8. Estimate awareness, treatment and control among participants with hypertension, diabetes and raised cholesterol.

9. Estimate the proportion with combined NCD risk factors and selected high-risk profiles.

10. Produce district, rural–urban, sex and age-stratified estimates with appropriate uncertainty.

 

3. RESEARCH QUESTIONS

• What proportion of adults currently use tobacco or alcohol?

• What proportion has inadequate diet or insufficient physical activity?

• What is the prevalence of over-weight, obesity and central obesity?

• What proportion has raised blood pressure, raised glucose or abnormal lipids, including previously undiagnosed participants?

• Among persons with measured or self-reported diseases, what proportion is aware, treated and controlled?

• How do risk factors vary by age, sex, residence, district, education, occupation and socioeconomic position?

• What proportion has 0, 1, 2, 3 or ≥4 major NCD risk factors?

 

4. STUDY DESIGN AND SETTING

A population-based, cross-sectional survey will be conducted throughout West Bengal. The design will be stratified by rural/urban residence and allocated to districts or approved survey domains using population-proportionate methods.

 

5. STUDY POPULATION

5.1 Inclusion criteria

• Age 18–69 years on the date of interview.

• Usual resident at the selected address for at least 12 months.

• Able to understand the participant information and provide informed consent.

• Willing to complete the applicable survey steps.

 

5.2 Exclusion or deferral criteria

• Pregnancy.

• Severe acute illness, medical instability or physical frailty making participation unsafe.

• Severe cognitive or communication impairment.

• Temporary visitor or resident for less than 12 months.

• Refusal of consent or inability to complete consent.

 

Exclusion must not be used to remove difficult-to-reach groups merely because participation is inconvenient. Reasons for ineligibility, refusal, non-contact and incomplete steps will be documented using standard disposition codes.

 

6. SAMPLE SIZE AND ALLOCATION

The source proposal used:

 n = Z²pq/d² = 1.96² × 0.50 × 0.50 / 0.05² = 384.

After design effect 2, eight age–sex estimation domains and 80% anticipated response:

 384 × 2 × 8 / 0.80 = 7,680.
